subject: General
hook: Eight questions to ask your child over the winter break. None are about school.
body: Three weeks of proximity is the best diagnostic window a parent gets all year, and it closes in January.
slides: Eight questions for the winter break.
None of them are about school.
1. What's something you're better at than you were last year?
2. What do your friends think you're good at?
3. If you could drop one subject, which — and what would you do with the time?
4. Who explains things in a way that makes sense to you?
5. What's the hardest thing you did this term?
6. What did you want to try this year and didn't?
7. What do you think I worry about too much?
8. What would make next term better?
Number 7 is the one that will surprise you.

subject: Mathematics
hook: The twelve topics that carry the most marks in a Grade 10 maths paper.
body: Not all chapters are equal. If revision time is short, these are where it should go, roughly in order of marks carried.
slides: Twelve topics. Most of the marks.
If revision time is short, spend it here.
1. Algebraic manipulation — appears inside almost everything else.
2. Linear and quadratic equations.
3. Trigonometry — right-angled first, then the rules.
4. Mensuration: surface area and volume.
5. Coordinate geometry.
6. Statistics: mean, median, mode from grouped data.
7. Probability — the tree diagram questions.
8. Similarity and congruence.
9. Circles: theorems and arc length.
10. Ratio, proportion and percentage.
11. Number: HCF, LCM, surds, indices.
12. Simple and compound interest.
Comment MATHS for the marks-per-topic breakdown.

subject: General
hook: Exam morning: the six things that actually change the score.
body: Everything else is superstition. These six are worth real marks and cost nothing.
slides: Exam morning. Six things that change the score.
Everything else is superstition.
1. EAT. Working memory runs on glucose. This is not a cliché.
2. NO NEW CONTENT. Anything learned this morning displaces something solid.
3. ARRIVE EARLY ENOUGH TO BE BORED. Rushing costs the first ten minutes of the paper.
4. READ THE WHOLE PAPER FIRST. Two minutes. Decide the order.
5. START WITH A QUESTION YOU CAN DO. Not question 1. One you can DO.
6. WATCH THE CLOCK AT THE HALFWAY MARK. Only then. Not every five minutes.
Notice that five of the six have nothing to do with knowing the subject.
That's usually where the missing marks are.

subject: English
hook: How we teach a child to mark their own work, and why it's the whole game.
body: A student who can mark accurately no longer needs anyone in the room. That's the actual goal of tutoring, and almost nobody teaches it explicitly.
slides: We teach children to mark their own work.
A student who can mark accurately doesn't need anyone in the room.
STEP 1 — They answer. We say nothing.
STEP 2 — They get the mark scheme. Not the answer. The mark scheme.
STEP 3 — They mark it themselves, out loud, saying why each mark is or isn't there.
STEP 4 — We only intervene where their marking is wrong.
What this builds: the examiner's voice in their head.
By week eight they're catching their own errors before we see them.
That's the point at which tutoring should start winding down. We say so.

subject: Science
hook: Every science definition you need, in one revision method.
body: Definitions are free marks that students lose because they revise them by reading. Reading is the one method that doesn't work here.
slides: Science definitions are free marks.
Students lose them because they revise by READING.
THE METHOD — three columns on one page.
COLUMN 1: the term. COLUMN 2: your definition from memory. COLUMN 3: the textbook's.
Write column 2 before you look at column 3. Always.
Where they differ is your revision list. Nothing else is.
Do ten terms a day. It takes twelve minutes.
Reading definitions creates recognition. This creates recall.
Only one of those is examined.

subject: General
hook: Signs it's the school, not your child.
body: Parents almost always look inward first. Sometimes that's wrong, and staying too long costs more than moving.
slides: Signs it's the school, not your child.
Parents look inward first. Sometimes that's the wrong direction.
1. The same complaint from several unconnected families.
2. Marks that dropped across ALL subjects at once, in one term.
3. Teacher turnover mid-year in a core subject.
4. 'She needs to try harder' with no specifics — repeatedly, from different staff.
5. Your child was fine at the last school.
6. Homework that is copying, not thinking, for months.
None of these on its own means much. Three of them together does.
Ask other parents before you ask your child again.

subject: Coding
hook: A first coding project that isn't a tutorial. Five evenings.
body: Tutorials teach syntax. Projects teach problem-solving, and only one of those transfers. Here's a first one that any 10-14 year old can finish.
slides: A first coding project. Not a tutorial. Five evenings.
Tutorials teach syntax. Projects teach problem-solving.
EVENING 1 — Decide what it does. Write it in one sentence, on paper.
EVENING 2 — Make the ugliest possible version that works. No styling.
EVENING 3 — Break it on purpose. Feed it bad input. Watch it fail.
EVENING 4 — Fix what broke. This is the evening that teaches the most.
EVENING 5 — Show someone. Explain a decision you made.
Good first projects: a quiz, a dice game, a units converter, a to-do list.
Bad first project: anything with a tutorial video attached.
Comment CODE for the parent primer.

subject: General
hook: Everything we won't do. A list, so you can hold us to it.
body: Most tutoring promises are about what will happen. These are the commitments that are easier to check.
slides: Everything we won't do.
Easier to check than a promise about results.

We won't send you 'great session today!' with nothing in it.

We won't keep a mentor who isn't the right fit for your child.
We won't chase you. One follow-up, then we leave you alone.
If we break any of these, say so. Free trial class — link in bio.

subject: Mathematics
hook: Squaring numbers near 100, without writing anything down.
body:
97². How far below 100? Three. Subtract that from the number: 97 − 3 = 94. That's the front. Square the difference: 3² = 9, written as two digits, 09. That's the back.

9409.

96² → 96−4 = 92, and 4² = 16 → 9216. It works because of one algebraic identity, which is exactly why identities are worth learning.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): '97 squared. No pen.'
STEP 1 (4-14s): 'How far below 100? Three. Take three off the number: 94. Front half.'
STEP 2 (14-24s): 'Square the difference. Three squared is nine. Write it as 09. Back half.'
ANSWER (24-32s): '9409.'
SECOND (32-44s): '96 squared. 96 minus 4 is 92. 4 squared is 16. 9216.'
CTA (44-52s): 'One identity does all of this. That's why identities are worth learning.'

subject: English
hook: Active voice, spotted in three seconds: add 'by zombies'.
body:
If you can put 'by zombies' after the verb and the sentence still works, it's passive.

'The window was broken by zombies.' Works — passive.
'The boy broke the window by zombies.' Nonsense — active.

It sounds like a joke. It is also the fastest reliable test anyone has found, and it survives into A-level.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): 'Active or passive? Add by zombies.'
TEST (4-14s): 'If you can put by zombies after the verb and it still works — it's passive.'
DEMO (14-30s): On screen: 'The window was broken BY ZOMBIES.' Works. Passive. / 'The boy broke the window BY ZOMBIES.' Nonsense. Active.
CLOSE (30-42s): 'It sounds like a joke. It's also the fastest reliable test anyone has found — and it works right through A-level.'

subject: Science
hook: Why a heavy thing and a light thing hit the ground together.
body:
Heavier objects are pulled harder — but they're also harder to move. The two effects cancel exactly.

Double the mass, double the force, same acceleration. That's not a coincidence, it's what makes gravity different from every other force a student meets.

Drop a textbook and a pencil, flat, from the same height. They land together and nobody quite believes it the first time.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'Heavy thing, light thing. Same height. They land together.'
WHY (5-22s): 'Heavier objects are pulled harder — but they're also harder to move. The two effects cancel. Exactly.'
MATH (22-34s): 'Double the mass, double the force, same acceleration.'
POINT (34-46s): 'That's not a coincidence. It's what makes gravity different from every other force they'll meet.'
CTA (46-54s): 'Textbook and a pencil. Flat. Try it tonight.'

subject: General
hook: Don't ask if they revised. Ask what they got wrong.
body:
'Did you revise?' has one honest answer and one easy one, and you'll get the easy one.

'What did you get wrong?' cannot be answered without having actually engaged with something. It's unfaultable as a question and impossible to bluff.

It also changes what revision means in your house — from time served to errors found.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'Don't ask if they revised. Ask what they got WRONG.'
WHY (5-18s): 'Did you revise has one honest answer and one easy one. You'll get the easy one.'
CONTRAST (18-32s): 'What did you get wrong can't be answered without actually engaging with something. It's impossible to bluff.'
CLOSE (32-46s): 'It also changes what revision means in your house. From time served, to errors found.'

subject: Mathematics
hook: Two negatives, one number line, no rules to memorise.
body:
Subtracting is walking left. Subtracting a negative is being told to walk left, backwards — which is walking right.

5 − (−3): start at 5, face left, walk backwards three. You land on 8.

Children who are taught 'two minuses make a plus' forget it under pressure. Children who can see the walk don't.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'Five minus negative three. Without the rule.'
SETUP (5-16s): Draw a number line. 'Subtracting is walking LEFT.'
TURN (16-30s): 'Subtracting a NEGATIVE is being told to walk left — backwards. Which is walking right.'
DEMO (30-42s): 'Start at 5. Face left. Walk backwards three. You land on 8.'
CLOSE (42-52s): 'Two minuses make a plus gets forgotten under pressure. The walk doesn't.'

subject: Public Speaking
hook: Where to look when you're speaking, so it isn't terrifying.
body:
Eye contact advice usually makes children worse, because scanning a room while thinking is genuinely hard.

Simpler: pick three people — left, middle, right. One sentence each, then move. That's it.

To the audience it reads as confident and deliberate. To the speaker it's three friendly faces instead of four hundred, which is a manageable number.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'Where to look while speaking, so it isn't terrifying.'
PROBLEM (5-16s): 'Standard eye contact advice makes kids worse. Scanning a room while thinking is genuinely hard.'
METHOD (16-32s): 'Pick three people. Left, middle, right. One sentence each, then move.'
PAYOFF (32-46s): 'To the room it looks deliberate. To the speaker it's three faces instead of four hundred.'
CTA (46-52s): 'Have them try it on the family first.'

subject: General
hook: Read the mark scheme. Not the textbook. The mark scheme.
body:
Every board publishes them, free, alongside the past papers. They tell you the exact words that earn marks — and often that a whole family of phrasings does not.

Students revise from textbooks and are then marked against a document they've never read.

One evening with three mark schemes changes how a child writes answers for the rest of the year.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'Read the mark scheme. Not the textbook. The mark scheme.'
FACT (5-18s): 'Every board publishes them free, next to the past papers. They tell you the exact words that earn marks.'
GAP (18-32s): 'Students revise from textbooks — then get marked against a document they've never read.'
ACTION (32-46s): 'One evening with three mark schemes changes how a child writes answers for the rest of the year.'
CTA (46-52s): 'Download three tonight. They're free.'

subject: French
hook: Fifty French words you already know, because English borrowed them.
body:
Any English word ending in -tion is almost always identical in French, with a different pronunciation. Nation, situation, attention, information, éducation.

-ible and -able transfer too: possible, terrible, capable, adorable.

A Grade 6 student walking into French thinking they know nothing is starting from about two thousand words. Telling them that on day one changes the whole year.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'You already know about two thousand French words. Nobody told you.'
RULE 1 (5-20s): 'Anything ending in -tion is almost always identical. Nation. Situation. Attention. Information.'
RULE 2 (20-32s): '-ible and -able transfer too. Possible. Terrible. Capable. Adorable.'
POINT (32-46s): 'A Grade 6 walking in thinking they know nothing is actually starting from two thousand words.'
CTA (46-54s): 'Comment FRENCH for the list.'

subject: General
hook: The child who finishes first is not the one who understands most.
body:
Speed feels like mastery and is often the opposite. Finishing early usually means skipping the checking, or not noticing the parts that deserved slowing down for.

Meanwhile the child who finishes last is frequently the one doing the most thinking, and gets told to hurry up.

In a house, praise the checking, not the finishing. It costs nothing and it changes what a child optimises for.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'The child who finishes first is not the one who understands most.'
BODY (5-20s): 'Speed feels like mastery. It's often the opposite — finishing early usually means skipping the checking.'
FLIP (20-34s): 'Meanwhile the child finishing last is frequently doing the most thinking. And gets told to hurry up.'
CLOSE (34-48s): 'Praise the checking, not the finishing. It costs nothing, and it changes what they optimise for.'

subject: Coding
hook: If your child can explain a bug, they've learned more than if the code worked.
body:
Working code teaches you that it worked. A bug you diagnosed teaches you how the machine actually thinks, which is transferable to every language they'll ever touch.

So the question after a coding session isn't 'did it work'. It's 'what broke, and why'.

A child who can answer that is doing computer science. A child whose code ran first time might just be copying.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-6s): 'If your child can explain a bug, they've learned more than if the code had worked.'
WHY (6-22s): 'Working code teaches you that it worked. A bug you diagnosed teaches you how the machine actually thinks.'
TRANSFER (22-34s): 'And that transfers to every language they'll ever touch.'
QUESTION (34-48s): 'So don't ask did it work. Ask what broke, and why.'
CTA (48-54s): 'Comment CODE for the parent primer.'

subject: Science
hook: Osmosis, using a raisin and a glass of water.
body:
Put a raisin in water overnight. It swells, because water moves from where there's more of it into where there's less, through the skin.

Put a grape in very salty water instead. It shrivels — same rule, opposite direction.

Two glasses, one night. Every Grade 9 biology student who has watched this happen stops mixing up which way osmosis goes.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'Osmosis. One raisin, one glass of water, one night.'
DEMO A (5-18s): 'Raisin in plain water. It swells. Water moves from where there's MORE of it to where there's less.'
DEMO B (18-32s): 'Grape in very salty water. It shrivels. Same rule, opposite direction.'
PAYOFF (32-46s): 'Two glasses. One night. And they stop mixing up which way osmosis goes — permanently.'
CTA (46-52s): 'Set it up before bed. Look in the morning.'

subject: General
hook: The revision technique with the best evidence is the one nobody enjoys.
body:
Spaced retrieval. Test yourself, get things wrong, wait a few days, test again.

It is uncomfortable, it feels unproductive, and it consistently outperforms re-reading, highlighting and summarising by a wide margin in study after study.

The discomfort is the mechanism, not a side effect. Anything that feels smooth is probably familiarity, not learning.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'The revision technique with the best evidence is the one nobody enjoys.'
NAME (5-14s): 'Spaced retrieval. Test yourself. Get it wrong. Wait days. Test again.'
EVIDENCE (14-30s): 'It feels unproductive. It consistently beats re-reading, highlighting and summarising — by a wide margin, study after study.'
KEY (30-46s): 'The discomfort IS the mechanism. Anything that feels smooth is familiarity, not learning.'
CTA (46-52s): 'Send this to someone highlighting a textbook.'

subject: Mathematics
hook: 'I'm just not a maths person' is a sentence with a date on it.
body:
Ask when they decided. Almost every child can tell you — a teacher, a test, a moment in Grade 4 or 6 where they concluded something permanent about themselves from one bad afternoon.

That belief then does the work. They stop trying on hard questions, which produces exactly the evidence that confirms it.

Finding the date is often the whole intervention. It turns an identity back into an incident.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-6s): 'I'm just not a maths person. That sentence has a date on it.'
ASK (6-18s): 'Ask when they decided. Almost every child can tell you. A teacher. A test. One bad afternoon in Grade 4.'
MECHANISM (18-34s): 'Then the belief does the work. They stop trying on hard questions — which produces the evidence that confirms it.'
CLOSE (34-50s): 'Finding the date is often the whole intervention. It turns an identity back into an incident.'

subject: English
hook: Write the last line first. It fixes most weak essays.
body:
If you know where you're ending, every paragraph has somewhere to go. If you don't, you write until you run out of time and call it a conclusion.

So: before the introduction, write the final sentence. The one thing you want the examiner holding when they put the pen down.

Then build backwards. Weak essays wander because nobody decided the destination.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'Write the last line first. It fixes most weak essays.'
WHY (5-20s): 'If you know where you're ending, every paragraph has somewhere to go. If you don't, you write until time runs out and call it a conclusion.'
METHOD (20-34s): 'Before the introduction — write the final sentence. The thing you want the examiner holding when they stop reading.'
CLOSE (34-48s): 'Then build backwards. Essays wander because nobody decided the destination.'

subject: General
hook: The session where we tell a child they were right and the textbook is confusing.
body:
It happens more than you'd think. A child's objection is often a sharper piece of thinking than the explanation they were given.

When a mentor says 'no, you're right, that book explains it badly' — something changes. The child stops assuming that confusion is a personal failing.

That single reframe does more for a struggling student than a term of extra practice.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-6s): 'Sometimes a mentor's job is to say: you're right, the textbook is confusing.'
FREQUENCY (6-18s): 'It happens more than you'd think. A child's objection is often sharper thinking than the explanation they were given.'
EFFECT (18-34s): 'And when someone says it out loud, the child stops assuming confusion is a personal failing.'
CLOSE (34-48s): 'That reframe does more for a struggling student than a term of extra practice.'

subject: Mathematics
hook: Ratio questions get easy the moment you find the one part.
body:
Split ₹4,500 in the ratio 4:5. Almost every mistake here comes from trying to do it in one step.

Add the parts: 4 + 5 = 9. Find one part: 4500 ÷ 9 = 500. Then multiply out: 4 × 500 = 2000, 5 × 500 = 2500.

One part. Always find one part first. It converts every ratio question in the syllabus into two multiplications.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'Split 4,500 in the ratio 4 to 5. Most mistakes happen in the first three seconds.'
CAUSE (5-14s): 'Because people try to do it in one step.'
METHOD (14-32s): 'Add the parts. 4 plus 5 is 9. One part is 4500 over 9 — that's 500. Then multiply out. 2000 and 2500.'
RULE (32-46s): 'Always find ONE PART first. It turns every ratio question in the syllabus into two multiplications.'
CTA (46-52s): 'Save it before the next test.'

subject: General
hook: A tired child cannot be taught. That's physiology, not attitude.
body:
Working memory — the part that holds a new idea long enough to use it — is one of the first things sleep debt takes away.

So an extra hour of tuition at 9pm on a school night is often a net negative. You're teaching a system that has switched off the component you need.

If something has to give in December, it isn't sleep. It's one of the activities.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'A tired child cannot be taught. That's physiology, not attitude.'
MECHANISM (5-20s): 'Working memory — the part that holds a new idea long enough to use it — is one of the first things sleep debt takes.'
CONSEQUENCE (20-36s): 'So an extra hour of tuition at 9pm is often a net negative. You're teaching a system with that component switched off.'
CLOSE (36-50s): 'If something has to give in December, it isn't sleep. It's one of the activities.'

subject: Science
hook: Speed, distance, time — and why the triangle is doing them harm.
body:
The triangle gets marks in Grade 8 and collapses in Grade 11, because it's a memory aid, not an understanding.

What survives: speed is how much distance per one unit of time. Say it that way and the formula rebuilds itself — 90 km in 2 hours is 45 km per one hour.

A child who understands 'per' can derive every rate formula in physics. A child with a triangle has one.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-6s): 'The speed-distance-time triangle is doing your child harm.'
WHY (6-20s): 'It gets marks in Grade 8 and collapses in Grade 11. It's a memory aid, not an understanding.'
INSTEAD (20-36s): 'Speed is how much distance per ONE unit of time. 90 kilometres in 2 hours is 45 per one hour.'
PAYOFF (36-50s): 'A child who understands PER can derive every rate formula in physics. A child with a triangle has one.'

subject: General
hook: Do the past paper before you finish revising. Not after.
body:
Everyone saves papers for the end, as a test. That wastes them.

A paper attempted early — badly, with gaps — tells you exactly what to revise. A paper attempted at the end only tells you whether the guessing worked.

Use the first two as diagnostics and expect a bad score. The score isn't the point; the map is.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'Do the past paper BEFORE you finish revising. Not after.'
PROBLEM (5-16s): 'Everyone saves papers for the end, as a test. That wastes them.'
BETTER (16-32s): 'A paper attempted early — badly, with gaps — tells you exactly what to revise. One done at the end only tells you if the guessing worked.'
CLOSE (32-46s): 'Use the first two as diagnostics. Expect a bad score. The score isn't the point. The map is.'

subject: General
hook: What a mentor does in the last five minutes decides whether the hour worked.
body:
Not a summary. A retrieval.

Book shut, notes away: tell me the three things we did, and do one of them. If that fails, the hour didn't land, and we'd rather find out now than next week.

Most tutoring ends with 'any questions?' — which reliably produces 'no', from a tired child who wants to leave.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-6s): 'What a mentor does in the last five minutes decides whether the hour worked.'
NOT (6-14s): 'Not a summary. A retrieval.'
METHOD (14-30s): 'Book shut. Notes away. Tell me the three things we did — and do one of them.'
WHY (30-42s): 'If that fails, the hour didn't land. Better to know now than next week.'
CONTRAST (42-54s): 'Most tutoring ends with any questions? Which reliably gets no, from a tired child who wants to leave.'

subject: General
hook: Handwrite the notes. The slower speed is the entire benefit.
body:
Typing is fast enough to transcribe without processing. Handwriting isn't — you physically cannot keep up, so you're forced to decide what matters and compress it.

That compression is the learning. The notes themselves are almost a by-product.

Which is also why copying someone else's notes does very little, however neat they are.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'Handwrite the notes. The slower speed is the whole point.'
CONTRAST (5-20s): 'Typing is fast enough to transcribe without processing. Handwriting isn't — you can't keep up.'
MECHANISM (20-34s): 'So you're forced to decide what matters and compress it. That compression IS the learning.'
COROLLARY (34-48s): 'Which is why copying someone else's notes does almost nothing. However neat they are.'

subject: Science
hook: She can do the practice questions and fails the test. That gap is predictable.
body:
Practice questions come in a chapter, so the method is given away by the page they're on. A test mixes topics, and suddenly the hard part isn't solving — it's recognising which tool to reach for.

That's a separate skill, and almost nobody practises it deliberately.

The fix: mixed sets. Twenty questions from five different chapters, shuffled. It feels much harder because it is the real task.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-6s): 'She can do the practice questions and fails the test. That gap is predictable.'
CAUSE (6-22s): 'Practice questions sit inside a chapter — the page gives away the method. A test mixes topics.'
SKILL (22-36s): 'So the hard part isn't solving. It's recognising which tool to reach for. Separate skill. Almost nobody practises it.'
FIX (36-50s): 'Mixed sets. Twenty questions, five chapters, shuffled. Feels much harder — because it's the real task.'

subject: Public Speaking
hook: Reading aloud at home is the cheapest exam-technique practice there is.
body:
Fifteen minutes of reading out loud builds three things at once: fluency, comprehension pacing, and tolerance for hearing your own voice — which is most of what stops a child speaking in class.

It costs nothing, needs no materials, and works from age six to sixteen.

Anything counts. A news article, a recipe, the back of a cereal box. The volume matters more than the text.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-6s): 'Reading aloud at home is the cheapest exam technique practice there is.'
THREE (6-24s): 'Fifteen minutes builds three things at once. Fluency. Comprehension pacing. And tolerance for hearing your own voice.'
POINT (24-36s): 'That last one is most of what stops a child speaking in class.'
CLOSE (36-50s): 'Costs nothing. Works from six to sixteen. A news article, a recipe, a cereal box — the volume matters more than the text.'

subject: General
hook: January is when everyone starts. That's precisely why December is better.
body:
In January every tutor is full, every good slot is taken, and your child begins alongside a wave of others who all left it late.

Starting in December means the diagnosis is done before the rush, the mentor has room, and week one of January is week four of the work.

Same effort. Three weeks of head start. It's the cheapest advantage in the calendar.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-6s): 'January is when everyone starts. Which is exactly why December is better.'
JANUARY (6-20s): 'In January every tutor is full, every good slot is taken, and your child starts alongside a wave of people who all left it late.'
DECEMBER (20-36s): 'Start in December and the diagnosis is done before the rush. The mentor has room.'
PAYOFF (36-48s): 'Week one of January becomes week four of the work. Same effort, three weeks ahead.'
CTA (48-56s): 'Free trial class. Link in bio.'

subject: Mathematics
hook: What a maths report tells you, and what it hides.
body:
A maths report is an average of averages.

62 percent might be strong algebra and collapsed geometry, or steady mediocrity across everything. Those need opposite responses, and the number cannot tell them apart.

Ask for the question-level breakdown. Most schools have it and rarely send it unprompted.

That one request changes the whole conversation.
slides: What a maths report tells you, and what it hides.
A percentage is an average of averages
'Could apply himself' usually means one topic
Effort grades measure compliance, not learning
Ask for the question-level breakdown
Save this before the next report evening.

subject: Public Speaking
hook: Nobody is confident the first time.
body:
Shyness sounds like a personality, which makes it sound permanent. Unrehearsed is a state, and states change.

The difference between a child who freezes and a child who presents is usually eight rehearsals nobody scheduled.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): Nobody is confident the first time.
BEAT (4-12s): Shyness is a personality. Unrehearsed is a state.
BEAT (12-20s): One sounds permanent. The other takes four weeks.
BEAT (20-29s): Nobody is fluent the first time they speak in front of people.
BEAT (29-34s): They are fluent the ninth time.
BEAT (34-43s): The gap is not courage. It is practice nobody scheduled.
CTA (43-48s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Coding
hook: Nine finished tutorials is not learning to code.
body:
Copying a tutorial line by line teaches typing. The learning happens when something breaks and a child has to work out why, and nothing in a finished tutorial ever breaks.

Ask what happens in week three when the code will not run.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): Nine finished tutorials is not learning to code.
BEAT (4-9s): Copying a tutorial teaches typing.
BEAT (9-15s): The learning happens when it breaks.

subject: Mathematics
hook: The Year 9 decision most parents make by accident.
body:
Set placement decides which tier your child is entered for, and the tier caps the grade available. That narrows what they can take at A Level, years before anyone mentions A Levels.

Most families find out on results day.

Ask which tier your child is on track for. Ask in Year 9, not Year 11.

subject: Coding
hook: What to actually teach a child about AI.
body:
Not prompting. Prompting will be obsolete in two years and it was never the hard part.

The durable skill is judgement: knowing when the answer is wrong, where it came from, and when the tool should stay closed. A child who can spot a confident wrong answer is more employable than one who can write a clever prompt.

That skill is just critical thinking with a new surface. Which is good news, because we already know how to teach it.

subject: French
hook: Why your child can pass French and still not speak it.
body:
Why a child can score well in French and still freeze in Paris.

Written exams reward recall. Speaking requires retrieval under time pressure, which is a different skill using a different part of the memory, and almost nothing in a school term practises it.

A vocabulary list learned on Sunday and tested on Friday is stored, not owned.

Ask when your child last had to answer a question in French without knowing it was coming.

Things you can date are things you can undo.

subject: Science
hook: Four science questions that reveal whether a child understands.
body:
Four questions that reveal whether a child understands science or has memorised it.

None of them ask for a definition. A definition can be recited by a child who has understood nothing, which is why exams stopped rewarding them.

These four ask what the idea is connected to. Understanding is a shape, not a fact, and you can only see the shape from the edges.

Try one tonight over dinner. Two minutes, no marking, and you will know more than the last report told you.

Where have you seen this outside the book?

What would you measure to test it?

subject: Mathematics
hook: The five-minute check that finds the gap.
body:
Five minutes, and no marking.

Give your child a question they already got right, and ask why the method works. Fluency without understanding shows up in seconds, and it is the best early warning there is.

Then set one from two years earlier. Watch where they pause, not what they answer.

The hesitation is the diagnosis.

subject: Coding

body:
Getting stuck is the subject, not an interruption to it.

Every professional developer spends most of the day with something not working. A child who thinks being stuck means being bad at it quits around week three.

Say it out loud early.

subject: Public Speaking
hook: What to say the night before they present.
body:
What to say the night before your child presents.

'Just be confident' asks them to produce a feeling on demand, which nobody can do. It reads as pressure, not support.

What works is specific and physical. Name the part they know best, so they have somewhere solid to start. Tell them nobody can see nerves, because it is true and they assume otherwise. And tell them to go slower than feels right, because speed is what nerves do to a voice and slowing down is the only lever they can actually pull mid-sentence.

subject: Coding
hook: Your child used AI for their homework. Now what?
body:
Your child used AI for their homework. The ban does not work.

It only moves the behaviour somewhere you cannot see, and removes your ability to teach anything about it.

What works is asking them to explain the work without the screen. The gap shows up in about ninety seconds, and it shows up to them, not just to you. That is a far better lesson than a rule.

Then agree what the tool is allowed to do next time. Explain a concept, yes. Write the paragraph, no. Children keep rules they helped write.

body:
The first one does most of the work. If the answer is 'start the syllabus', walk away - it assumes the problem is coverage, and it almost never is.

A good tutor names a measure before they begin. 'More confident' is not a measure. 'She will close negative numbers in three weeks' is.

And listen carefully to the third answer. Explaining again, louder, is not teaching. Going backwards to find the missing step is.

Find the gap first. Then the hours count.

subject: French

They are checking tense control, justified opinions, and whether you can keep going when a word will not come.

Every candidate loses a word mid-sentence. The mark difference is whether they stop dead or say it another way.

subject: Public Speaking
hook: How to fix a child who rushes when nervous.
body:
Nerves do not make a child quiet. They make a child fast.

And speed is the thing that costs marks, because nobody can follow it and the speaker cannot hear themselves think.

Telling them to slow down does not work under pressure. Marking the pauses on the page does, because it turns a feeling into an instruction.

The first line matters most. Rehearse it until it is automatic, and the rest arrives on a body that has already started.

subject: Coding
hook: How to tell a real coding class from an expensive one.
body:
Ask to see a student project from week eight, not the showreel. Week eight is where the difference lives: either everyone's project looks identical, which means they copied, or they look different, which means they built.

Ask what happens when a child finishes early. In a good class, they extend it. In a weak one, they wait.

And ask how many students share a screen. Two is fine, and often better. Four means three are watching.

subject: Mathematics
hook: The two topics everything else is built on.
body:
Two topics carry almost everything after them.

Fractions in Year 7. Negative numbers in Year 8. Ratio, algebra, trigonometry and calculus all sit on top of them, and neither gets formally revisited once the class has moved on.

So a shaky Year 7 becomes a difficult Year 11, and it looks like the student got worse. They did not. The foundation was always thin and the building got taller.

It is not ability. It is sequence, and sequence problems have solutions.

Negative numbers, around Year 8

Yes, and more urgently than before. The skill now is telling when the answer is wrong, and that is subject knowledge, not technology.

You cannot audit an answer in a subject you do not understand.

Three questions for a school tour the brochure will not answer.

The third matters most. A school that puts its strongest teacher with students who are struggling believes ability can move. One that gives the bottom set to whoever is free has already decided it cannot.

subject: Public Speaking
hook: Four moments speaking decides the outcome.
body:
Speaking is the only school subject that is also every subsequent interview.

And almost nobody trains for it, because it does not appear on a report card. It appears at nineteen, in a room, when the grades have already done their job and something else is being assessed.

The useful thing about it is that it responds to practice faster than almost anything else on a timetable. Four weeks of deliberate work changes how a child sounds. Four weeks of maths rarely changes a grade.

Start earlier than feels necessary.

Re-reading a vocabulary list is comfortable, so nothing is being strengthened. Covering it and writing it from memory feels worse and works.

Memory grows at the point of effortful recall.

subject: Mathematics
hook: What to say when they get a bad mark.
body:
What to say when the mark comes back low.

'Did you revise?' is a trial, and children defend themselves in trials rather than think. You will get a defence, not information.

Every question in this list points at the paper instead of the child, which is where the useful information is. 'Was it the topic or the timing' in particular separates two completely different problems that produce identical marks.

And 'show me the one you nearly got' is the fastest route back to a child who has stopped talking about it.

subject: Science
hook: Why practicals matter more than the mark suggests.
body:
Practicals carry more weight than their share of the marks suggests.

Method questions appear across every paper, and they are answered well by students who have actually stood over an experiment that did not work. You can revise a method. You cannot revise the instinct for what usually goes wrong.

There is a second reason. Ten years later, the mole calculations are gone and the afternoon the reaction turned an unexpected colour is still there.

A subject people remember is a subject people carry on with.

They are where the theory becomes falsifiable

It is the only part students remember in ten years

subject: Coding

body:
Every child should build one thing other people actually use.

The shift happens the first time someone reports a bug. The work has consequences outside the classroom, and they stop asking whether it is finished and start asking whether it works.

subject: General
hook: What a good session actually looks like.
body:
What a good session actually looks like from the outside.

The student talks more than the tutor. That single ratio separates teaching from lecturing, and it is easy to check - just ask your child who did most of the talking.

Something goes wrong on purpose, because a student who has only seen worked examples has never practised the actual skill, which is recovering.

And it ends with something they can do without help. Not something they watched. Something they can do.

body:
No child is behind. A topic was left unfinished, and everything after it inherited the gap.

That is not a kindness, it is a diagnosis. One version makes a fourteen year old the problem. The other makes it a sequence, and sequences can be reordered.

subject: Mathematics
hook: Reading worked examples is not revision.
body:
The answer is already on the page, so nothing is retrieved and nothing sticks. It gets filed under 'seen', which is not the same as 'can do'.

Close the book. Start the question. Being stuck is the part that teaches.

subject: Public Speaking
hook: What to say the night before a presentation.
body:
'You'll be fine' closes the conversation. It sounds like reassurance and lands like a door shutting, because the child still has the fear and now has nowhere to put it.

Name it instead. 'Most people go blank somewhere in the middle. What do you do if that happens?' turns a vague dread into one thing with a plan attached.

Then ask for the first line out loud, once. The opening is where the nerves live, and hearing it in a kitchen makes the classroom quieter.

hook: Six languages is not six times the learning.
body:
Syntax is the cheapest part of programming and the easiest to look up. What transfers between languages is decomposition, naming, testing and reading an error properly.

One language, held long enough to finish something that runs, teaches every one of those.

subject: French
hook: Four reasons French vocabulary will not stick.
body:
Most lists get learned French to English, because that is the direction the test runs. Then the speaking assessment asks for the opposite and the word is not there.

Words also arrive stripped of context. 'Chercher' on a list is a translation. 'Je cherche mes clés' is a memory, and memories survive longer than translations.

And almost none of it is said aloud, so the mouth has never made the sound under pressure.

Same twenty words. Both directions, in sentences, out loud, twice across a week. That is the whole change.

subject: Coding

body:
Something should run on the first day. Not a slide about what programming is, not an hour of theory about variables. Working code, on screen, that the student can point at.

And something should break on the first day, deliberately, while there is a teacher in the room. A child who has only ever seen code work has never practised the actual job.

Then the error message gets read out loud rather than scrolled past. Most beginners never learn that the computer already told them what was wrong.

subject: Coding
hook: How to ask about the AI without starting a row.
body:
'Did you use AI for this?' is an accusation with a yes-or-no exit, and both answers end the conversation.

'What did it get wrong?' does not. It assumes use, skips the confession, and lands straight on the only skill that matters: whether your child can spot a confident sentence that is untrue.

'What did you type to get that?' is the second good question. The prompt shows the thinking. A vague prompt means the tool did the work; a specific one means your child did.

And set the rule between deadlines. Nobody negotiates well at eleven at night.

Without a method children sweep the room, land on nobody and look more nervous than when they started.

subject: Mathematics
hook: A Level Maths does not start in Year 12.
body:
A Level Maths does not start in Year 12. It starts with algebraic fluency in Year 10.

The first term assumes rearranging, factorising, surds and indices are automatic, and moves at a pace that does not allow for relearning them. A student who can do that algebra slowly and carefully is, in that room, a student who cannot do it.

This is why strong IGCSE grades sometimes turn into a difficult October. The grade measured whether they could get there. A Level measures whether they can get there without thinking about it.

The fix belongs to the summer between, and it is narrow: fluency drills on the algebra they already know.

Reading is recognition with time attached. Speaking is recall against a clock, choosing a verb ending live, in front of someone. A child can be strong in one and lost in the other.

subject: Science
hook: Combined or separate sciences: what actually changes.
body:
Separate sciences are usually more content rather than harder content, and they cost a timetable slot that has to come from somewhere. Often that somewhere is a language or a humanity your child would have enjoyed.

The decision that matters is not prestige, it is what your child wants at A Level and what your specific sixth form asks for. Entry requirements differ between schools, so the only reliable answer comes from the school itself.

Ask that question directly, in Year 9, and take the answer in writing. It converts an anxious guess into a scheduling decision.
slides: Combined or separate sciences: what actually changes.
Separate sciences cover more content, not harder content
Three sciences means three slots on the timetable
Combined keeps a language or a humanity alive
Neither closes A Level Sciences by itself
Ask the school what their sixth form expects.

subject: Coding
hook: Red text is not a telling-off.
body:
The error message is the most specific piece of help available, and most beginners never read it. Eyes slide off, hands go up.

One habit fixes it: say the message out loud before touching the keyboard. Being stuck becomes a procedure instead of an emergency.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): Red text is not a telling-off.
BEAT (4-11s): The instinct is to feel caught and look away.
BEAT (11-19s): The line number goes unread. The message goes unread.
BEAT (19-28s): But that message is the most specific help in the session.
BEAT (28-37s): Written by the machine, free, at the exact moment it is needed.
BEAT (37-46s): The habit: say it out loud before touching the keyboard.
CTA (46-51s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Mathematics
hook: The marks were lost in the working, not the answer.
body:
Method marks reward a visible process. A wrong final value with three correct written steps can outscore a bare answer that happened to be right.

Write the substitution. Write the rearrangement. It costs four seconds a question.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): The marks were lost in the working, not the answer.
BEAT (4-10s): Examiners mark a process, not a number.
BEAT (10-19s): Three visible correct steps can outscore a bare right answer.
BEAT (19-27s): Students who work in their heads lose this quietly.
BEAT (27-32s): Tidy books. Inexplicable marks.
BEAT (32-41s): Write the substitution. Write the rearrangement. Four seconds.
CTA (41-46s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Coding
hook: Same tool. One child gets weaker, one gets stronger.
body:
The difference is the request. 'Answer this' hands over the thinking. 'Give three approaches, then compare them' keeps it, and keeps the child practising the part no tool supplies.

Banning it usually just moves it somewhere unsupervised.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): Same tool. One child gets weaker, one gets stronger.
BEAT (4-11s): The difference is the shape of the request.
BEAT (11-17s): 'Answer this' hands over the thinking.
BEAT (17-25s): 'Give three approaches, then compare them' keeps it.
BEAT (25-34s): One learns the tool is smarter. One learns judgement is the product.
BEAT (34-39s): Ask for options, not answers.
CTA (39-44s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Public Speaking
hook: A speaking assessment is not testing charisma.
body:
It tests structure: a position, two reasons, back to the position. Then whether that position survives a follow-up question, which is where most students fold.

Children who look naturally good at this are simply practised.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): A speaking assessment is not testing charisma.
BEAT (4-11s): Position, two reasons, back to the position.
BEAT (11-20s): That sounds prepared even when it is invented on the spot.
BEAT (20-27s): Then: does the position survive one follow-up?
BEAT (27-36s): That is where most students fold and agree with the examiner.
BEAT (36-44s): None of it is personality. All of it is a drill.
CTA (44-49s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Mathematics
hook: More practice will not fix a misunderstanding.
body:
Repetition makes a wrong method faster and harder to unlearn. A child getting the same kind of question wrong is not under-practised, she is confidently doing something that does not work.

Watch one question out loud. Find the step. Then practise.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): More practice will not fix a misunderstanding.
BEAT (4-10s): Practice makes a correct method faster.
BEAT (10-16s): It makes an incorrect method faster too.
BEAT (16-25s): And much harder to remove, because it has been rehearsed.
BEAT (25-32s): Watch one question being done out loud instead.
BEAT (32-40s): The broken step is usually visible in ninety seconds.
CTA (40-45s): Follow for the rest.

subject: French
hook: The Sunday hour is mostly recovery.
body:
Language memory fades daily, so a week-long gap means opening with twenty minutes of re-warming. Four ten-minute contacts keep the sound in the mouth.

Same total time. Different subject by half term.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): The Sunday hour is mostly recovery.
BEAT (4-12s): Language fades on a daily clock, not a weekly one.
BEAT (12-19s): So twenty minutes go on ground already covered.
BEAT (19-27s): Four short contacts keep the sound in the mouth.
BEAT (27-36s): Pronunciation is muscular. Muscles are not maintained weekly.
BEAT (36-45s): Ten minutes is small enough that nobody argues about it.
CTA (45-50s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Coding
hook: A coding club is not a coding course.
body:
A club is designed so a child who missed last week still enjoys this week. That constraint is exactly what makes progression impossible.

Ask what week eight assumes that week one taught. If nothing, it is exposure, not a course.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): A coding club is not a coding course.
BEAT (4-13s): A club is exposure, and that is worth having at eleven.
BEAT (13-22s): But a club is built so that missing a week costs nothing.
BEAT (22-29s): Which means the difficulty can never rise.
BEAT (29-35s): A course has an order and a next thing.
BEAT (35-43s): Ask what week eight assumes that week one taught.
CTA (43-48s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Science
hook: The wrong prediction is the useful one.
body:
When predictions get written after the results, the experiment stops being an experiment. Nothing can surprise anyone, and surprise is where the learning was.

A wrong prediction honestly recorded is better work than a right one copied off the board.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): The wrong prediction is the useful one.
BEAT (4-11s): Students learn to write the safe prediction.
BEAT (11-17s): Or to write it after the results arrive.
BEAT (17-24s): At that point nothing can surprise anyone.
BEAT (24-32s): And surprise is where the understanding was hiding.
BEAT (32-41s): What did the model get wrong? That is the whole subject.
CTA (41-46s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Mathematics
hook: Same grade. Completely different next year.
body:
A grade built on remembered procedures and one built on understood procedures look identical on results day. They stop looking identical the first time a question arrives in an unfamiliar shape.

Ask why the method works. 'That's just how you do it' is the fragile answer.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): Same grade. Completely different next year.
BEAT (4-13s): A grade can be built on remembered procedures or understood ones.
BEAT (13-20s): The paper often cannot tell the difference.
BEAT (20-27s): Then a question arrives in an unfamiliar shape.
BEAT (27-36s): One student adapts. One waits to be told which method this is.
BEAT (36-45s): Ask why the method works. The answer tells you which you have.
CTA (45-50s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Coding
hook: How AI actually gets used in a lesson.
body:
To generate eight variations of the question that exposed the gap. To play the student a child has to teach. To produce a confident wrong answer worth arguing with.

Never to produce work that gets handed in. That inverts the point.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): How AI actually gets used in a lesson.
BEAT (4-13s): As a supply of practice: eight versions of one question type.
BEAT (13-19s): As a student the child has to teach.
BEAT (19-27s): The questions it asks back expose what they missed.
BEAT (27-35s): As an opponent, producing a confident wrong solution.
BEAT (35-42s): Never to produce work that gets handed in.
CTA (42-47s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Public Speaking
hook: The quiet child in class is often the loudest at home.
body:
Not personality. Audience. The fluency is already there; what changed is the cost of being wrong in front of thirty peers.

One prepared sentence offered early in the lesson does more than a term of being told to speak up.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): The quiet child in class is often the loudest at home.
BEAT (4-11s): That is not personality. That is audience.
BEAT (11-16s): The fluency is already there.
BEAT (16-25s): What changed is the cost of being wrong in front of thirty peers.
BEAT (25-32s): So do not aim for brave. Aim for rehearsed.
BEAT (32-41s): One prepared sentence, offered early, beats a term of 'speak up'.
CTA (41-46s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Mathematics
hook: The Year 11 problem started in Year 7.
body:
Fractions get marked as done and then quietly underpin ratio, probability, rates and every algebraic fraction that follows. Marks lost across several unrelated topics are often one gap, four years upstream.

Ask for three-quarters divided by two-fifths tonight, with the reasoning out loud.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): The Year 11 problem started in Year 7.
BEAT (4-11s): Fractions arrive early and get marked as done.
BEAT (11-20s): Then they hold up ratio, probability, rates and rearranging.
BEAT (20-29s): The topic never leaves. It stops being called fractions.
BEAT (29-38s): Marks lost across unrelated topics are often one gap, upstream.
BEAT (38-43s): Nobody reteaches it after Year 8.
CTA (43-48s): Follow for the rest.

subject: French
hook: Do not correct the accent at the dinner table.
body:
A child speaking French at home is producing language with no script, in front of the audience that matters most. Interrupting to fix a vowel makes speaking riskier than silence.

Correction belongs in the lesson. Accuracy has a whole term to arrive.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): Do not correct the accent at the dinner table.
BEAT (4-13s): A child speaking French at home is doing the hardest thing there is.
BEAT (13-22s): No script, in front of people whose opinion actually matters.
BEAT (22-31s): Fix a vowel and speaking now carries a risk silence does not.
BEAT (31-36s): So the sentence stops coming.
BEAT (36-45s): Correction belongs in the lesson. At home, keep it coming.
CTA (45-50s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Coding
hook: A ban is a position, not a policy.
body:
Ask what is allowed, what must be declared, and how assessment has changed in response. The last one matters most, because it is the only answer that costs the school something.

Ask for the document. A school that has one will hand it over.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): A ban is a position, not a policy.
BEAT (4-10s): It says what the school disapproves of.
BEAT (10-18s): Not what happens to a piece of homework on a Tuesday.
BEAT (18-27s): A policy names what is allowed and what must be declared.
BEAT (27-34s): And how assessment has changed in response.
BEAT (34-43s): That last part is the only one that costs the school something.
CTA (43-48s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Coding
hook: Scratch is not a toy that gets outgrown.
body:
Loops, conditionals, variables and events are the same concepts a first computer science course teaches. Text adds syntax, and syntax is the cheap part.

Move across when the blocks become the slow part, not when the calendar says so.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): Scratch is not a toy that gets outgrown.
BEAT (4-12s): Loops, conditionals, variables, events, sequence.
BEAT (12-19s): Those are first-year computer science concepts.
BEAT (19-28s): What text adds is syntax, and syntax is not the hard part.
BEAT (28-37s): Push a child out early and they fight semicolons instead of structure.
BEAT (37-45s): Move across when the blocks become the slow part.
CTA (45-50s): Follow for the rest.

subject: General
hook: The term report arrives this month. Read it in this order.
body: Most parents read top to bottom and land on the number. The useful information is somewhere else entirely.
slides: The term report lands this month.
Read it in this order, not top to bottom.
1. TEACHER COMMENTS FIRST. Specific comments mean they know your child. Generic ones mean they don't.
2. THE SPREAD, not the average. 80 in one subject and 45 in another is a different problem to 62 across the board.
3. CHANGE since last term. Direction matters more than position.
4. EFFORT vs ATTAINMENT. High effort, low attainment is a teaching problem. The reverse is a motivation one.
5. THE NUMBER. Last. It's a summary, not a diagnosis.
Then ask the school for the question-level breakdown. Most have it.
Comment EXAM for the questions to bring to the meeting.

subject: Mathematics
hook: 'She's fine, she just needs to practise more.' Ask which twenty minutes.
body:
Practice is not one thing. Twenty minutes on questions she can already do builds confidence and nothing else. Twenty minutes on the one topic she avoids is where the marks are.

Children, sensibly, choose the first. Nobody volunteers for the uncomfortable one.

So the question isn't whether she practises. It's whether anyone is choosing what she practises.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'She just needs to practise more. Okay — which twenty minutes?'
SPLIT (5-20s): 'Twenty minutes on what she can already do builds confidence and nothing else. Twenty on the topic she avoids is where the marks are.'
WHY (20-32s): 'Children choose the first. Every time. Nobody volunteers for the uncomfortable one.'
CLOSE (32-44s): 'The question isn't whether she practises. It's whether anyone is choosing what she practises.'

subject: General
hook: The December slump is real, and it isn't laziness.
body:
By week fourteen of a term, most children are running on empty. Attention drops, marks wobble, and the household reads it as attitude.

It's usually accumulated fatigue meeting the hardest content of the year, because syllabuses back-load the difficult chapters into the term nobody has energy left for.

The right response is triage, not pressure. Pick one subject. Leave the others to coast for three weeks.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'The December slump is real. It isn't laziness.'
BODY (5-20s): 'By week fourteen most children are running on empty. Attention drops, marks wobble, and everyone reads it as attitude.'
INSIGHT (20-36s): 'It's fatigue meeting the hardest content of the year — because syllabuses back-load the difficult chapters into the term nobody has energy left for.'
ADVICE (36-50s): 'Triage, not pressure. Pick ONE subject. Let the others coast for three weeks.'
CTA (50-54s): 'Send this to a tired parent.'

subject: Science
hook: Four sentences on a report card, and what each one actually means.
body: Report comments are written under time pressure, in a shared vocabulary. Once you know the code they're surprisingly direct.
slides: Four report card sentences. Decoded.
They're written fast, in a shared vocabulary. The code is readable.
'Could apply himself more' → usually one specific topic he's avoiding. Ask which.
'A pleasure to teach' → lovely, and tells you nothing academic. Ask a second question.
'Would benefit from consolidating basics' → there is a real gap below this year's work.
'Participates well in class' → check whether this survives written work. Often it doesn't.
None of these are criticisms of your child.
All four are invitations to ask one more question.

subject: English
hook: He can talk about the book brilliantly and writes half a page. That gap has a cause.
body:
Speaking is generative and forgiving — you can start a sentence without knowing where it ends. Writing is committed. Every sentence is permanent and judged.

Children who talk well and write badly are usually not short of ideas. They're short of a method for getting an idea out of their head and onto a page in a fixed order.

That method is teachable in about six weeks, and it's mostly planning, not vocabulary.

subject: Mathematics
hook: Two children, same 58. Completely different winters ahead.
body:
Child A got 58 by doing well on the first half of the paper and running out of time. Child B got 58 spread evenly, understanding roughly half of everything.

A has a pacing problem, fixable in about three weeks of timed papers. B has a comprehension problem, and that's a term.

The number is identical. The response should be nothing alike. This is why the mark, on its own, is nearly useless.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'Two children. Both got 58. Completely different winters ahead.'
A (5-18s): 'Child A did well on the first half and ran out of time.'
B (18-30s): 'Child B scored evenly — understanding about half of everything.'
TURN (30-44s): 'A has a pacing problem. Three weeks of timed papers. B has a comprehension problem. That's a term.'
CLOSE (44-54s): 'Same number. Opposite response. Which is why the mark alone is nearly useless.'
CTA (54-58s): 'Comment MATHS for the diagnostic.'

subject: General
hook: Winter break: what actually helps, and what just ruins the holiday.
body: Three weeks off is long enough to lose fluency and short enough that cramming achieves nothing. There is a middle setting.
slides: Winter break. Three weeks.
Long enough to lose fluency. Too short for cramming to work.
DON'T: a full revision timetable. It won't survive week one, and failing it costs more than it gains.
DON'T: nothing at all. Arithmetic fluency and language recall genuinely decay.
DO: twenty minutes, four days a week, on ONE weak topic. That's it.
DO: read anything. Fiction counts. Comprehension is built by volume, not by worksheets.
DO: let them be bored. Boredom is where the recovery happens.
A rested child in January beats a resentful one who did more.

subject: General
hook: Comparing your child to their sibling is the most expensive sentence in the house.
body:
It never produces effort. It produces a story: I'm the one who isn't good at this.

Once a child holds that story, low marks stop being information and start being confirmation, and they'll protect the story by not trying — because not trying is a safer explanation for failing than trying and failing.

Compare a child to themselves last term. Nothing else.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'Comparing your child to their sibling is the most expensive sentence in the house.'
WHY (5-18s): 'It never produces effort. It produces a story: I'm the one who isn't good at this.'
MECHANISM (18-36s): 'Once that story exists, low marks stop being information and start being confirmation. And they'll protect it by not trying — because not trying is a safer explanation than trying and failing.'
FIX (36-48s): 'Compare a child to themselves last term. Nothing else.'

subject: Public Speaking
hook: Annual day is coming. The child with the small part is learning more than you think.
body:
Parents worry about the size of the role. Children mostly worry about whether they'll be embarrassed.

A three-line part, delivered without freezing, in front of four hundred people, does more for a child's willingness to speak in class in January than a lead role learned in panic.

Ask about the freezing, not the lines.

subject: Coding
hook: 'He's on the laptop all evening.' Ask what he's making.
body:
There is an enormous difference between consuming and building, and from the doorway they look identical.

A child watching gameplay and a child modding a game are in completely different developmental positions, and the second one is doing something closer to homework than you'd guess.

The question that separates them takes four seconds: show me what you made.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'He's on the laptop all evening. Okay — ask what he's MAKING.'
CONTRAST (5-20s): 'Consuming and building look identical from the doorway. A child watching gameplay and a child modding a game are in completely different places.'
POINT (20-34s): 'The second one is doing something much closer to homework than you'd guess.'
CLOSE (34-44s): 'The question that separates them takes four seconds. Show me what you made.'

subject: General
hook: What our mentors do in December that they don't do in August.
body:
August is diagnosis and gap-filling. December is protection.

By now a child has a term of accumulated fatigue, a report card they've read, and mocks in sight. Sessions get shorter and more targeted, we stop introducing new material three weeks before an exam, and we spend more time on what they already half-know.

Same mentor, different job. Teaching that ignores the calendar is teaching that ignores the child.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'What our mentors do in December that they don't do in August.'
AUGUST (5-15s): 'August is diagnosis and gap-filling.'
DECEMBER (15-32s): 'December is protection. A term of fatigue, a report card they've read, mocks in sight. Sessions get shorter and more targeted.'
RULE (32-46s): 'We stop introducing new material three weeks before an exam. We work on what they already half-know.'
CLOSE (46-56s): 'Same mentor, different job. Teaching that ignores the calendar ignores the child.'

subject: General
hook: Five things our mentors are told never to say.
body: Every one of them is well-meant. Every one of them costs something.
slides: Five things our mentors are told never to say.
All well-meant. All expensive.
'It's easy.' — If they can't do it, you've just told them what that makes them.
'You should know this by now.' — Shame doesn't teach. It closes the session.
'Just remember it.' — If memory were the problem, they'd have done it.
'We're behind.' — Adds urgency to a child who already feels it. Manage the schedule quietly.
'Your brother found this fine.' — Never. Not once.
What they say instead: 'Show me what you tried.'

subject: General
hook: We ask every mentor to teach the same topic badly on purpose. Here's what it reveals.
body:
In the trial we give them a topic and a student who is quietly lost, and we watch what they do when the first explanation doesn't land.

Weak teachers say the same thing again, louder and slower. Good ones change the representation entirely — a diagram, an analogy, a smaller number.

The first explanation is easy. What you're hiring is the second and third.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-6s): 'We ask every mentor to teach a topic to someone who is quietly lost. Then we watch.'
TEST (6-20s): 'What matters isn't the first explanation. It's what they do when it doesn't land.'
WEAK (20-32s): 'Weak teachers repeat themselves. Louder. Slower.'
GOOD (32-46s): 'Good ones change the representation completely. A diagram. An analogy. A smaller number.'
CLOSE (46-56s): 'The first explanation is easy. What you're hiring is the second and the third.'

subject: General
hook: If your child likes their mentor but the marks haven't moved, say so.
body:
It's the hardest message for a parent to send, because the relationship is working and nobody wants to be the one who breaks it.

Send it anyway. Warmth without progress is a pleasant hour, and after two months it's an expensive one.

Usually it's a method problem, not a person problem, and it's fixable in a conversation. Occasionally it isn't, and then we change the mentor. Either way, week eight is the moment to raise it — not month five.

subject: General
hook: The note that goes home after a session your child found hard.
body: The easy weeks write themselves. This is the template for the difficult ones, because that note is where trust is either built or lost.
slides: The note after a session that went badly.
The easy weeks write themselves. This one matters more.
1. NAME IT PLAINLY. 'Today was hard. She got three of eight.'
2. SAY WHAT IT MEANS. 'That's the transposition gap, not the chapter.'
3. SAY WHAT'S NEXT. 'Two more sessions on this before we go back.'
4. SAY WHAT NOT TO DO. 'Please don't quiz her on it tonight.'
5. NO REASSURANCE PADDING. She'll be fine helps nobody.
A parent who gets this note stops guessing.
A parent who gets 'good session today!' starts.

subject: Mathematics
hook: Multiply any two-digit numbers in the fifties, in your head.
body:
Both in the fifties? 54 × 57.

Add the units to 25: 4 + 7 = 11 → 25 + 11 = 36. That's the front.
Multiply the units: 4 × 7 = 28. That's the back.

3628.

53 × 56 → 25+9 = 34, and 3×6 = 18 → 3418. It works because both numbers sit either side of fifty, and fifty squared is a very friendly number.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): '54 times 57. In your head. Watch.'
STEP 1 (4-16s): 'Add the units to 25. Four plus seven is eleven. 25 plus 11 is 36. That's the front.'
STEP 2 (16-26s): 'Multiply the units. Four times seven is 28. That's the back.'
ANSWER (26-34s): '3628.'
SECOND (34-46s): '53 times 56. 25 plus 9 is 34. 3 times 6 is 18. 3418.'
CTA (46-52s): 'Works for anything in the fifties. Show a kid tonight.'

subject: English
hook: How to plan an essay in four minutes, so the writing takes half as long.
body: Most students write to find out what they think. Four minutes of planning turns that into writing down what they already decided, which is a completely different task.
slides: Plan an essay in four minutes.
Then the writing takes half as long.
MIN 1 — Answer the question in ONE sentence. That's your position.
MIN 2 — List three reasons it's true. Just three words each.
MIN 3 — Next to each, note the evidence. Quote, event, figure.
MIN 4 — Order them: second-strongest, weakest, strongest. Finish hard.
Now write. You're transcribing a decision, not making one.
Students who skip this write for 40 minutes and discover their argument in the last paragraph.

subject: Science
hook: Why you feel colder in water than in air at the same temperature.
body:
20°C air feels mild. 20°C water feels freezing. The temperature is identical — what changes is the rate.

Water conducts heat away from your skin roughly 25 times faster than air, so your body loses warmth far quicker even though the water isn't colder.

This is the difference between temperature and heat transfer, and it's the single idea most Grade 8 students never quite separate.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): '20 degree air feels mild. 20 degree water feels freezing. Same temperature.'
QUESTION (5-14s): 'So what's different?'
ANSWER (14-30s): 'The RATE. Water pulls heat off your skin about 25 times faster than air. You're not colder. You're losing warmth quicker.'
PAYOFF (30-44s): 'That's the difference between temperature and heat transfer — the one idea most Grade 8 students never separate.'
CTA (44-50s): 'Save it for the next physics chapter.'

subject: Mathematics
hook: Six marks students throw away in every maths paper, and how to stop.
body: None of these are about knowing more maths. All of them are about not donating marks you've already earned.
slides: Six marks thrown away in every maths paper.
None of them are about knowing more maths.
1. NO UNITS. cm, kg, seconds. One mark, every time.
2. NO WORKING SHOWN. Right answer, no method — you lose the method marks.
3. ROUNDING TOO EARLY. Round at the END, or the final answer drifts.
4. NOT ANSWERING THE QUESTION ASKED. You found x. It wanted the area.
5. BLANK SPACE. An attempt scores more than nothing. Always write something.
6. NOT CHECKING THE MARK ALLOCATION. 4 marks means four things to say.
Comment EXAM for the checklist to tape inside a pencil case.

subject: French
hook: The French past tense, decided by one question.
body:
Passé composé or imparfait? Ask: is this a photograph or a film?

A photograph is a finished moment — j'ai mangé, I ate. Passé composé.
A film is background, ongoing, repeated — je mangeais, I was eating, I used to eat. Imparfait.

'Il pleuvait quand je suis sorti.' It was raining — film. I went out — photograph. Both in one sentence, and now you can hear why.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'Passé composé or imparfait? One question settles it.'
QUESTION (5-12s): 'Is this a photograph, or a film?'
PHOTO (12-24s): 'A photograph is a finished moment. J'ai mangé. I ate. Passé composé.'
FILM (24-36s): 'A film is background, ongoing, repeated. Je mangeais. I was eating. Imparfait.'
BOTH (36-50s): 'Il pleuvait quand je suis sorti. It was raining — film. I went out — photograph. Both in one sentence.'
CTA (50-56s): 'Comment FRENCH for the tense sheet.'

subject: General
hook: Revise the thing you got wrong, not the subject you're worried about.
body:
Anxiety picks the subject. Evidence should pick the topic.

Most students spend December revising the subject that scares them, which is often not the one leaking the most marks. The error log knows; the feeling doesn't.

Open the last three tests. Count the lost marks by topic. Revise the top two. Everything else waits.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'Revise what you got wrong. Not the subject you're worried about.'
POINT (5-18s): 'Anxiety picks the subject. Evidence should pick the topic. They're rarely the same.'
METHOD (18-34s): 'Open the last three tests. Count lost marks by topic. Revise the top two.'
CLOSE (34-46s): 'Everything else waits. The error log knows where the marks are. The feeling doesn't.'

subject: Public Speaking
hook: How to structure any two-minute talk, in four lines.
body: Children over-prepare content and under-prepare shape. Shape is what makes it feel confident.
slides: Any two-minute talk. Four lines.
Kids over-prepare content and under-prepare shape.
LINE 1 — The claim. 'Homework should be optional after Grade 8.'
LINE 2 — The reason. 'Because it stops measuring learning and starts measuring compliance.'
LINE 3 — The example. One. Specific. Real.
LINE 4 — The return. Say the claim again, in different words.
That's it. Everything else is filling in the middle.
A talk with shape sounds confident even when the speaker isn't.
Comment SPEAK for the practice drills.

subject: Coding
hook: Variables, explained with a shoebox. Works on any eight-year-old.
body:
A variable is a labelled box. You write a name on the outside — score — and put something inside. Later you can look in, or swap what's in there for something else.

The name stays. The contents change. That's the whole idea, and it's the thing children actually get stuck on.

Give them three boxes and some paper. Ten minutes of that beats an hour of syntax.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'Variables. Explained with a shoebox. Works on any eight-year-old.'
BODY (5-20s): Hold up a box with SCORE written on it. 'Write a name on the outside. Put something in. Later, look in — or swap it for something else.'
KEY (20-32s): 'The name stays. The contents change. That's the whole idea.'
WHY (32-44s): 'And it's exactly where children get stuck — they think the name IS the thing.'
CTA (44-52s): 'Three boxes and some paper. Ten minutes beats an hour of syntax.'

subject: Mathematics
hook: The 15% tip trick that teaches percentages better than a worksheet.
body:
10% is moving the decimal point. 5% is half of that. Add them.

Bill of ₹840? 10% is 84. Half of 84 is 42. So 15% is 126.

What makes this teach so well is that it breaks an awkward percentage into two easy ones — which is the actual skill percentages are testing, and the one worksheets rarely make visible.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): '15% of 840. No calculator. Five seconds.'
STEP (4-16s): '10 percent is just moving the decimal. 84. Five percent is half of that. 42.'
ADD (16-24s): 'Add them. 126.'
WHY IT TEACHES (24-40s): 'The real skill is breaking an awkward percentage into two easy ones. That's what the exam is testing. Worksheets rarely make it visible.'
CTA (40-48s): 'Do it out loud at the next restaurant bill.'

subject: English
hook: Cut every 'very' and watch the writing get older.
body:
'Very sad' is weaker than 'devastated'. 'Very big' is weaker than 'vast'. 'Very tired' is weaker than 'exhausted'.

The word 'very' is a signal that a better word exists and hasn't been found yet. So it becomes a search prompt, not a crime.

Have your child underline every 'very' in their last essay and replace it. Vocabulary marks move within a fortnight.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): 'Cut every very. The writing gets two years older.'
EXAMPLES (4-20s): On screen: very sad → devastated. very big → vast. very tired → exhausted.
REFRAME (20-34s): 'Very is a signal that a better word exists and hasn't been found yet. It's a search prompt, not a crime.'
HOMEWORK (34-46s): 'Underline every very in the last essay. Replace it.'
CTA (46-52s): 'Vocabulary marks move inside a fortnight.'

subject: Science
hook: Graph questions are free marks. Here's the order to answer them in.
body: Almost every science paper has one, and almost every student loses marks in the same four places.
slides: Graph questions are free marks.
Most students lose them in the same four places.
1. READ THE AXES FIRST. Including the units and the scale. Ten seconds.
2. STATE THE TREND before the numbers. 'As X increases, Y decreases.'
3. QUOTE DATA. Two points, with units. This is where the marks are.
4. NAME THE ANOMALY if there is one. Examiners put it there on purpose.
5. ONLY THEN explain WHY, if asked.
Students do 5 first and skip 3. That's the lost mark, every time.
Trend → data → anomaly → explanation. In that order.

subject: General
hook: Teach it to someone. It's not a study tip, it's a test.
body:
Explaining a topic out loud to another person exposes exactly where the understanding stops, because you cannot bluff through a sentence you don't have.

The listener doesn't need to know the subject. A younger sibling, a parent, a wall. The value is in the speaking, not the audience.

Where they stumble is the revision list. Everything they explained fluently is already done.

subject: Mathematics
hook: Why dividing by a fraction makes the answer bigger.
body:
6 ÷ ½ = 12, and every child finds that offensive.

But read the question properly: how many halves fit inside six? Twelve. Obviously twelve.

Division has always meant 'how many of these fit inside that'. Nothing changed when the divisor became a fraction — only the intuition did, because we spend six years dividing by numbers bigger than one.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'Six divided by a half is twelve. Every child finds that offensive.'
REFRAME (5-18s): 'Read it properly. How many halves fit inside six? Twelve. Obviously twelve.'
POINT (18-34s): 'Division has always meant how many of these fit inside that. Nothing changed when the divisor became a fraction.'
WHY IT FEELS WRONG (34-48s): 'Only the intuition changed — because we spend six years dividing by numbers bigger than one.'
CTA (48-54s): 'Try the question on them tonight.'

subject: General
hook: Study with the phone in another room. Not face-down. Another room.
body:
Face-down still costs you. Research on this is unusually consistent: the presence of a phone reduces available attention even when it's silent and untouched, because part of the mind is spent not-checking it.

That's not weakness, it's load. You can't will it away, you can only remove the source.

Another room. Ninety minutes. The difference is measurable in a fortnight.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'Study with the phone in another room. Not face-down. Another room.'
EVIDENCE (5-20s): 'The research here is unusually consistent — a phone reduces available attention even when it's silent and untouched.'
WHY (20-34s): 'Because part of the mind is spent NOT checking it. That's not weakness. It's load.'
CLOSE (34-48s): 'You can't will it away. You can only remove the source. Another room. Ninety minutes.'

subject: General
hook: Board exams are in ten weeks. Here's the only schedule that survives contact.
body: Elaborate timetables fail in week one and the failure costs more than the plan was worth. This one is deliberately crude.
slides: Ten weeks to boards.
Elaborate timetables fail in week one. This one is crude on purpose.
WEEKS 10-8 — Past papers, untimed, open book. Find the gaps. Don't panic about scores.
WEEKS 7-5 — Close the book. Same papers. Now the score means something.
WEEKS 4-2 — Full papers, full time, in one sitting. Stamina is a separate skill.
WEEK 1 — Error log only. No new content. No new papers.
THROUGHOUT — One subject per day. Not three. Switching costs more than it looks.
Sleep is not the thing you cut. It's the thing that makes the rest work.
Comment EXAM for the printable version.

subject: General
hook: Your child's mock result is not a prediction. It's a measurement taken mid-treatment.
body:
