Mocks happen with weeks of syllabus still unfinished and revision barely started. Reading them as a forecast of the final grade is like weighing someone halfway through a diet and declaring the outcome.

What a mock is genuinely good for: showing which topics are unfinished, and how the pacing holds up under a real clock.

Use it for that. Then put the number away.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-6s): 'A mock result is not a prediction. It's a measurement taken mid-treatment.'
CONTEXT (6-20s): 'Mocks happen with syllabus unfinished and revision barely started.'
ANALOGY (20-32s): 'Reading it as a forecast is like weighing someone halfway through a diet and declaring the outcome.'
USE (32-46s): 'What it IS good for: which topics are unfinished, and whether pacing holds under a clock.'
CLOSE (46-54s): 'Use it for that. Then put the number away.'

subject: General
hook: Choosing streams after Grade 10: the four questions that actually matter.
body: This decision gets made on prestige and parental hope more often than on evidence. Four questions cut through most of it.
slides: Choosing streams after Grade 10.
Usually decided on prestige. Here's what evidence would say.
1. WHICH SUBJECT DOES SHE READ ABOUT WITHOUT BEING ASKED? Not which she scores highest in.
2. WHICH DEGREES REQUIRE WHICH SUBJECTS? Look it up. Actually look it up, this month.
3. WHAT DOES SHE DO WHEN A PROBLEM GETS HARD? Persist, or switch? That predicts more than marks.
4. WHAT'S REVERSIBLE? Science to commerce is easy. The other direction rarely is.
The honest one nobody asks: whose ambition is this?
A stream chosen for someone else is abandoned in the second year.

subject: General
hook: What examiners are told to do with an answer they can't read.
body: Handwriting isn't marked. But an examiner marking 300 scripts cannot award a mark for a word they cannot decipher, and they will not spend ninety seconds deciphering it.
slides: What examiners do with an answer they can't read.
Handwriting isn't marked. But this still costs.
An examiner marks ~300 scripts. Roughly 90 seconds each.
They cannot award a mark for a word they can't read.
And they will not spend the extra 60 seconds working it out.
THE FIX ISN'T NEATER WRITING. It's fewer, shorter sentences.
Number your points. Leave a line between them. Underline the key term.
A structured page is read faster and marked more generously.
This is worth more in December than another revision hour.

subject: Mathematics
hook: The calculator paper and the non-calculator paper need different revision. Most students do one.
body:
The non-calculator paper tests arithmetic fluency, estimation and number sense. The calculator paper tests method selection, multi-step reasoning and knowing what to type.

Revising 'maths' generally prepares you for neither specifically. Students who lose marks on paper 1 rarely lose them on paper 2 for the same reason.

Sort your lost marks by paper. The two lists look nothing alike.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-6s): 'The calculator paper and the non-calculator paper need different revision. Most students do one.'
PAPER 1 (6-18s): 'Non-calculator tests arithmetic fluency, estimation, number sense.'
PAPER 2 (18-30s): 'Calculator tests method selection, multi-step reasoning, knowing what to type.'
POINT (30-44s): 'Revising maths generally prepares you for neither. Students who lose marks on paper 1 rarely lose them on paper 2 for the same reason.'
CTA (44-54s): 'Sort your lost marks by paper. The two lists look nothing alike.'

subject: English
hook: The unseen text question, in the order an examiner wants it.
body: Students panic at unseen passages because they treat them as a comprehension test. They're a technique test, and technique can be prepared even when the text can't.
slides: The unseen text question.
You can't prepare the text. You can prepare the technique.
1. READ THE QUESTION FIRST. Then the passage. Never the other way round.
2. ANNOTATE FOR THE QUESTION ONLY. Ignore everything else, however interesting.
3. FIND THREE MOMENTS, spread across the passage. Beginning, middle, end.
4. FOR EACH: what the writer does, then WHY it works on a reader.
5. The 'why it works on a reader' is where almost all the marks live.
Most students describe the technique and stop. That's half a mark of a possible three.
Prepare the shape. The text takes care of itself.

subject: General
hook: IB students: your Extended Essay deadline is closer than the calendar says.
body:
The formal deadline is not the real one. The real one is the last week your supervisor has time to read a full draft and give you something you can act on.

That's usually three to four weeks earlier, and it's the difference between a grade band.

Ask your supervisor today: when do you need my complete draft to be able to comment properly? Then work back from that.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-6s): 'IB students — your Extended Essay deadline is closer than the calendar says.'
POINT (6-20s): 'The formal deadline isn't the real one. The real one is the last week your supervisor can read a FULL draft and give you something usable.'
GAP (20-32s): 'That's usually three to four weeks earlier.'
STAKES (32-42s): 'And it's the difference between a grade band.'
ACTION (42-54s): 'Ask them today: when do you need my complete draft to comment properly? Work back from that.'
CTA (54-58s): 'Comment IB for the guide.'

subject: Science
hook: Six-mark questions have a shape. Learn the shape, not more content.
body: Extended-response questions are marked on a band, not on a point count. Students who write more content and less structure score lower than students who do the reverse.
slides: Six-mark questions have a shape.
They're banded, not point-counted. Structure beats volume.
OPEN with the direct answer. One sentence. No preamble.
THEN the mechanism — the because. This is the largest band.
THEN a specific example or piece of data.
THEN the limitation, or the other side, if the command word invites it.
CLOSE by answering the question again in different words.
Five short paragraphs beats one long one, every time.
Practise the shape on a topic you know. Then it's automatic on one you don't.

subject: General
hook: January admissions: the three documents schools ask for that nobody prepares.
body:
Everyone prepares for the entrance test. Almost nobody prepares the rest, and the rest is where avoidable rejections happen.

A current transfer certificate and report set, obtained before the December break, not during the January rush.
A short parent statement — why this school, in your words, not a template.
And the child's own two minutes, because most schools interview and most children have never been asked why they want to come.

Prepare all three in November.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-6s): 'January admissions. Three things schools ask for that nobody prepares.'
ONE (6-18s): 'Current transfer certificate and reports. Get them BEFORE the December break, not in the January rush.'
TWO (18-30s): 'A short parent statement. Why this school, in your words. Not a template.'
THREE (30-44s): 'The child's own two minutes. Most schools interview — and most children have never been asked why they want to come.'
CLOSE (44-54s): 'Prepare all three in November. It's the cheapest advantage available.'

subject: General
hook: Grade boundaries move every year. What that means for your child.
body: Parents plan around a fixed number — 'she needs 75 for an A'. Boundaries are set after the papers are marked, against how the whole cohort performed.
slides: Grade boundaries move every year.
Parents plan around a fixed number. Boundaries aren't fixed.
They're set AFTER marking, against how the whole cohort did.
A hard paper lowers the boundary. An easy one raises it.
WHICH MEANS: a mark isn't a grade. Your child is being measured against a year group.
So 'she needs 75' is not a real target. It's last year's number.
THE USEFUL TARGET: comfortably above the boundary, not on it.
And a three-year boundary range, not a single figure, is what you should be planning with.
Ask the school for the last three years. They have them.

subject: General
hook: What eight weeks with a mentor looks like when it's working.
body: Not marks. Marks are the last thing to move. These are the signals that arrive first, in the order they arrive.
slides: Eight weeks in, when it's working.
Marks move last. These arrive first, in this order.
WEEK 2 — They stop saying 'I don't get any of it' and name a specific topic.
WEEK 3 — They attempt a question before asking for help.
WEEK 4 — They can say what they got wrong, not just that they got it wrong.
WEEK 6 — They correct themselves mid-answer. This one matters most.
WEEK 8 — A mark moves.
If you're at week six and none of these have happened, say so. Don't wait for week twelve.
This list is also how you judge any tutor, including us.

subject: Mathematics
hook: Why we spend the first December session doing nothing but past papers.
body: Not to test them. To watch them work under a clock, which is a different activity to teaching and reveals different things.
slides: The first December session is a past paper. Nothing else.
Not to test them. To WATCH them under a clock.
WHAT WE'RE LOOKING FOR — not the score.
Where do they stall? Which question do they skip and never come back to?
Do they read the whole paper first, or start at Q1 and hope?
How long before they abandon a question? Usually far too soon.
Do they check anything at the end, or put the pen down?
Every one of those is fixable in a fortnight — and none of them are maths.
Together they're usually worth more marks than the content revision.

subject: General
hook: Starting in December is not too late. Starting in February is.
body:
Ten weeks before boards, there is still time to fix pacing, close two topics and rebuild the habit of finishing a paper. Those are the highest-yield things available and they're all still open.

By February the only honest offer anyone can make is damage limitation.

One free class this month tells you which of those is actually on the table for your child.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-6s): 'Starting in December isn't too late. Starting in February is.'
DECEMBER (6-22s): 'Ten weeks out, you can still fix pacing, close two topics, and rebuild the habit of finishing a paper. Highest-yield things available.'
FEBRUARY (22-34s): 'By February the only honest offer anyone can make is damage limitation.'
CTA (34-48s): 'One free class this month tells you which of those is on the table. Link in bio.'

subject: General
hook: What we'd do with your child in the ten weeks before a board exam.
body: Written out plainly so you can compare it with anyone else you're considering, including doing nothing.
slides: Ten weeks before a board exam. What we'd actually do.
Written plainly, so you can compare it with anyone. Including doing nothing.
SESSION 1 — A full past paper. We watch. We don't teach.
SESSIONS 2-4 — The two topics costing the most marks. Only those two.
SESSIONS 5-8 — Timed sections. Pacing, not content.
SESSIONS 9-12 — Error log. Every mistake from the last eight weeks, re-attempted.
LAST 2 WEEKS — Nothing new. Consolidation and sleep.
WHAT WE WON'T DO: race through the whole syllabus again. There isn't time and it doesn't work.
Free trial class. Link in bio.

subject: General
hook: We're not taking new board-exam students after 15 December. Here's why that's not a sales line.
body:
Under ten weeks, the honest arithmetic stops working. There isn't room to diagnose properly, close a real gap and then build exam stamina on top — and a programme that skips the first step is just expensive revision.

We'd rather say no in December than take the money in January and manage your expectations in March.

If boards are this year and you're considering it, this month is the decision, not next.

subject: Mathematics
hook: Your child is not weak at Maths. They missed one chapter in Grade 6.
body:
Almost every Grade 9 algebra collapse traces back to one thing: fractions were never made automatic in Grade 6.

The child can do the new chapter. They just can't do the arithmetic underneath it fast enough, so the working memory runs out halfway through the sum and the answer comes out wrong.

The fix is not more Grade 9 practice. It is ten minutes a day on the Grade 6 gap, for about three weeks. Then Grade 9 stops feeling impossible.

Ask your child to simplify 3/4 + 2/5 without a pen. If they hesitate, you've found it.

subject: Science
hook: 78 in Science, but she can't explain photosynthesis at the dinner table.
body:
That gap has a name. It's called inert knowledge — facts that can be retrieved for a test and nowhere else.

It happens when a child learns to recognise questions instead of understanding ideas. The exam rewards it. Life doesn't.

The test for it is embarrassingly simple: ask them to explain the chapter to you like you're eight years old. If they can only recite, the marks are borrowed.

One question at dinner, twice a week. That's the whole intervention.
slides: 78 in Science.
Can't explain it at dinner.
This has a name: inert knowledge.
Facts that work in an exam and nowhere else.
It happens when a child learns to RECOGNISE questions, not understand ideas.
The test: 'Explain today's chapter like I'm eight.'
If they can only recite — the marks are borrowed.
Two dinner questions a week. That's the whole fix.

subject: English
hook: He reads fluently. He still scores 11 out of 20 in comprehension.
body:
Fluency and comprehension are two different skills, and Indian schooling tends to test the first while grading the second.

A child can decode every word on the page and still not hold the paragraph in their head long enough to answer a question about it.

What helps: after each paragraph, one sentence out loud — 'so what just happened?' It is slow for a week. Then it becomes silent, and automatic, and the comprehension marks move.

subject: Mathematics
hook: The five silent gaps that show up as 'careless mistakes'.
body:
No child is careless forty times in one paper. What looks like carelessness is almost always an automaticity gap — a step that should be free is costing effort.

Here are the five that account for most of it, in the order they usually appear.
slides: 'Careless mistakes' is a diagnosis nobody checks.
No child is careless 40 times in one paper.
GAP 1 — Times tables past 7. Every long sum leaks time here.
GAP 2 — Negative signs. Not the concept. The speed.
GAP 3 — Fractions to decimals, both directions, no pen.
GAP 4 — Transposing terms across the equals sign.
GAP 5 — Reading the question twice. Genuinely. Twice.
Fix the automaticity and the 'carelessness' disappears.
Comment MATHS — I'll send the full Grade 9 checklist.

subject: General
hook: Your child studied for six hours and remembers nothing. Here's why.
body:
Six hours of re-reading is not six hours of studying. Re-reading creates a feeling of familiarity that the brain misreads as knowing.

The switch is to close the book and write down what you remember, badly, from memory. It feels worse. It works about three times better.

Thirty minutes of recall beats three hours of highlighting. Every study on this says the same thing, and every child resists it, because it's uncomfortable — which is exactly the point.

subject: Mathematics
hook: 'I understood it in class' is the most expensive sentence in your house.
body:
Understanding in class is recognition. Solving alone is retrieval. They live in different parts of the brain and only one of them is examined.

The gap between the two is where most of a school year quietly disappears.

So change the question. Not 'did you understand?' — ask 'can you do one, right now, without looking?'

subject: Science
hook: Grade 8 Science is where most kids quietly decide they're 'not a science person'.
body:
It's the year the subject stops being stories about the world and starts being formulae, units and numerical problems.

Children who were curious at 12 become avoidant at 13, and everyone calls it 'losing interest'. It isn't. It's the arithmetic underneath physics arriving before anyone checked whether the arithmetic was ready.

Catch it in Grade 8 and it's a six-week fix. Catch it in Grade 11 and it's a different conversation entirely.

subject: General
hook: Seven things a report card cannot tell you.
body: A report card is a summary of outcomes. It contains almost no information about causes — which is the only thing a parent can actually act on.
slides: Seven things a report card cannot tell you.
1. Whether 62 was a ceiling or a bad week.
2. Whether they understood it or memorised the pattern.
3. Which chapter the gap actually started in.
4. Whether they asked for help and were rushed past.
5. Whether they can do it alone, or only with the class.
6. How much of the mark was handwriting and presentation.
7. Whether they still believe they can get better.
A report card gives you outcomes. You need causes.
Comment EXAM — I'll send the diagnostic questions to ask.

subject: Public Speaking
hook: She knows the answer. She won't raise her hand. That's not shyness.
body:
By Grade 6, most classroom silence is not personality. It is a risk calculation: the cost of being wrong in front of thirty people is higher than the reward of being right.

The child is being rational. The environment is the problem.

What changes it is low-stakes reps — speaking to one person, then three, then the room. Confidence is not a trait you're born with. It's a rep count.

subject: General
hook: Stop asking 'how was school'. Ask this instead.
body:
'How was school' gets you 'fine' for eleven years. It's a closed question wearing an open question's clothes.

Three that actually work: What did you get stuck on today? Who did you help? What did the teacher say that you didn't agree with?

The third one is the good one. It tells you whether your child is still thinking, or just receiving.

subject: Mathematics
hook: The 11 times table trick nobody teaches, and it works up to 99.
body:
Take any two-digit number. Split the digits. Add them. Put the sum in the middle.

32 × 11 → 3_2, 3+2=5 → 352.
45 × 11 → 4_5, 4+5=9 → 495.

If the middle sum crosses 9, carry it left. 87 × 11 → 8_7, 8+7=15 → carry the 1 → 957.

Teach it once. Your child will show it to everyone for a week, and that is exactly how a child decides Maths is interesting.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-3s): '32 times 11. Three seconds. Watch.'
DEMO (3-15s): Write 3 _ 2. 'Split the digits. Add them. Three plus two is five. Put it in the middle. 352.'
SECOND (15-24s): '45 times 11. Four, nine, five. 495.'
EDGE CASE (24-38s): '87? 8 plus 7 is 15. Carry the one. 957.'
CTA (38-44s): 'Show your kid tonight. They'll show everyone at school tomorrow.'

subject: English
hook: 'Its' and 'it's' — the rule that finally makes it stick.
body:
Forget everything about possession. Use one test.

Say the sentence with 'it is'. If it survives, you need the apostrophe. If it collapses, you don't.

'Its raining' → 'it is raining' → survives → it's raining.
'The dog wagged it's tail' → 'the dog wagged it is tail' → collapses → its tail.

One test. No grammar vocabulary. Works forever.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-3s): 'Its versus it apostrophe s. One test. Forever.'
RULE (3-12s): 'Say the sentence with IT IS. If it survives, apostrophe. If it collapses, no apostrophe.'
DEMO 1 (12-22s): On screen: Its raining → it is raining → survives → IT'S.
DEMO 2 (22-34s): The dog wagged it's tail → the dog wagged IT IS tail → collapses → ITS.
CTA (34-40s): 'Save it. You'll use it in an email this week.'

subject: Science
hook: Why the sky is blue — explained so a nine-year-old actually gets it.
body:
Sunlight is all colours mixed. When it hits the air, the tiny molecules bounce the short, jumpy wavelengths around far more than the long, lazy ones.

Blue is short and jumpy. So blue gets scattered across the whole sky, and you see it coming from everywhere at once.

At sunset the light travels through much more air, the blue is scattered away entirely before it reaches you, and the long lazy reds are all that survive the trip.

Same physics. Two different skies.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): 'Why is the sky blue? Not the textbook answer. The one a nine-year-old keeps.'
BODY (4-20s): Torch through a glass of milky water. 'Sunlight is all colours mixed. Air molecules bounce the short jumpy waves much more than the long lazy ones.'
PAYOFF (20-32s): 'Blue is short and jumpy. It gets thrown everywhere. So the sky is blue from every direction at once.'
TWIST (32-44s): Tilt the torch through more water. 'At sunset the light travels through way more air. The blue is scattered away before it reaches you. Only the lazy reds survive.'
CTA (44-48s): 'Same physics. Two skies. Save this one.'

subject: Mathematics
hook: Percentages in your head, in one line: x% of y = y% of x.
body:
They are the same number. Always.

4% of 75 looks awful. Flip it: 75% of 4 = 3. Done.
18% of 50? Flip it: 50% of 18 = 9.
16% of 25? Flip it: 25% of 16 = 4.

The rule is one multiplication written in a different order, which is why it's true — and why nobody thinks to use it.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): 'What is 4% of 75? Don't reach for the calculator.'
RULE (4-12s): 'x percent of y equals y percent of x. Always. Same number.'
DEMO (12-28s): 'So flip it. 75% of 4. That's 3. Done.' On screen: 18% of 50 → 50% of 18 → 9. And: 16% of 25 → 25% of 16 → 4.
WHY (28-38s): 'It works because it's the same multiplication, written in a different order.'
CTA (38-44s): 'Bookmark it. You'll use it on a restaurant bill.'

subject: French
hook: The French gender rule that covers about 80% of nouns.
body:
Nobody memorises 20,000 genders. They learn endings.

Masculine endings: -age, -ment, -eau, -isme, -oir. Le fromage, le moment, le bateau.
Feminine endings: -tion, -sion, -té, -ette, -ance, -ence. La nation, la beauté, la chance.

That covers most of what a Grade 6-10 student will meet. The exceptions get learned as exceptions, which is a much shorter list than the whole language.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): 'Stop memorising French genders one word at a time.'
BODY (4-10s): 'Learn the endings instead. Eighty percent of nouns follow them.'
LIST 1 (10-24s): On screen: -age, -ment, -eau, -isme, -oir → LE. Say: 'le fromage, le moment, le bateau.'
LIST 2 (24-38s): -tion, -sion, -té, -ette, -ance, -ence → LA. Say: 'la nation, la beauté, la chance.'
CTA (38-46s): 'Comment FRENCH — I'll send the full vocabulary pack.'

subject: Coding
hook: Teach a 10-year-old what a loop is, using a toothbrush.
body:
'Brush your teeth' is not one instruction. It's: move the brush, repeat 200 times, stop when the timer ends.

That's a loop. A thing you do, a number of times, until a condition is met.

Every child already runs dozens of loops a day. Coding just gives them the notation. Start there and 'programming' stops sounding like a foreign country.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): 'You can teach a ten-year-old what a loop is with a toothbrush.'
BODY (4-18s): Hold up toothbrush. 'Brush your teeth isn't one instruction. It's: move the brush. Repeat. Stop when the timer ends.'
NAME IT (18-30s): 'That's a loop. A thing you do, a number of times, until a condition is met. Write it on paper — they'll get it instantly.'
PAYOFF (30-40s): 'Kids already run dozens of loops a day. Coding just gives them the notation.'
CTA (40-46s): 'Comment CODE for the parent primer.'

subject: English
hook: Three words that make any school essay sound older than it is.
body:
However. Therefore. Nevertheless.

Not because they're fancy — because each one forces a relationship between two ideas. A child who writes 'therefore' has to prove a consequence. A child who writes 'however' has to hold a contrast.

The vocabulary is the smallest part. The thinking is the point. Examiners are marking the joint between the sentences, not the sentences.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): 'Three words that make a school essay sound two years older.'
REVEAL (4-12s): On screen, one by one: However. Therefore. Nevertheless.
WHY (12-28s): 'Not because they're fancy. Because each one forces a relationship. Write therefore and you have to prove a consequence. Write however and you have to hold a contrast.'
PAYOFF (28-38s): 'The examiner is marking the joint between your sentences. Not the sentences.'
CTA (38-44s): 'Save this before the next essay.'

subject: Mathematics
hook: Why a negative times a negative is positive — without saying 'it's a rule'.
body:
Watch the pattern and let it finish itself.

3 × 2 = 6. 3 × 1 = 3. 3 × 0 = 0. 3 × (-1) = -3. Each step down the second number drops the answer by 3.

Now do it with -3. -3 × 2 = -6. -3 × 1 = -3. -3 × 0 = 0. Each step down raises the answer by 3. So -3 × (-1) must be +3.

Nothing was memorised. The pattern had no choice.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): 'Negative times negative is positive. Not because it's a rule. Watch.'
PATTERN 1 (4-18s): Write on board, calling it out: 3×2=6, 3×1=3, 3×0=0, 3×(-1)=-3. 'Every step down drops the answer by three.'
PATTERN 2 (18-34s): -3×2=-6, -3×1=-3, -3×0=0. 'Now every step down RAISES it by three. So the next one has to be...' Write +3.
PAYOFF (34-42s): 'Nothing memorised. The pattern had no choice.'
CTA (42-46s): 'Show this to a kid who says maths makes no sense.'

subject: Public Speaking
hook: The pause is the technique. Everything else is decoration.
body:
Children speak fast when they're nervous because speed shortens the exposure. It also destroys everything they meant to say.

One drill: after every full stop, count one in your head before the next sentence. Silently. That's it.

It feels enormous to the speaker and completely normal to the room. Every good speaker your child has ever heard is doing this, and none of them mention it.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): 'The pause is the technique.' Pause a full beat. 'Everything else is decoration.'
WHY (4-16s): 'Kids speak fast when they're nervous because speed shortens the exposure. It also destroys the content.'
DRILL (16-30s): 'One drill. After every full stop — count one. Silently. Then the next sentence.'
REASSURE (30-40s): 'It feels enormous to them. It sounds completely normal to the room.'
CTA (40-46s): 'Comment SPEAK for the full drill sheet.'

subject: Science
hook: Balance any chemical equation with one rule: leave hydrogen and oxygen for last.
body:
Most students balance left to right and end up going in circles.

Order matters. Do the metals first. Then the non-metals that aren't H or O. Then hydrogen. Then oxygen, last, because oxygen appears in the most places and adjusts most easily.

Same equation, same chemistry, a third of the time. This one sequencing habit is worth several marks a paper.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): 'Balancing equations takes forever because you're doing it in the wrong order.'
RULE (4-14s): On screen: 1 Metals → 2 Other non-metals → 3 Hydrogen → 4 Oxygen LAST.
WHY (14-26s): 'Oxygen appears in the most places, so it adjusts most easily. Do it last and it falls into place instead of fighting you.'
DEMO (26-40s): Balance one combustion equation live using the order.
CTA (40-46s): 'Save this before your next chemistry test.'

subject: General
hook: Study 25 minutes, break 5. Not because it's trendy — because of what the break does.
body:
The break isn't rest. It's when the brain files what just happened.

Which is why the break has to be boring. Walking, water, staring out of a window. A five-minute scroll fills the exact space the filing needed and the session evaporates.

Same 25 minutes of work. Completely different retention. The phone is the variable, not the timer.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): '25 minutes on, 5 off. Everyone knows this. Almost everyone does it wrong.'
INSIGHT (4-16s): 'The break isn't rest. It's when the brain files what just happened.'
RULE (16-30s): 'Which is why the break has to be BORING. Walk. Water. Window. Not a scroll.'
PAYOFF (30-40s): 'Five minutes of feed fills the exact space the filing needed. Same work, no retention.'
CTA (40-46s): 'Send this to a teenager who studies with their phone face-up.'

subject: Mathematics
hook: Squaring any number ending in 5, in two seconds.
body:
Take the digits before the 5. Multiply by the next number up. Stick 25 on the end.

35² → 3 × 4 = 12 → 1225.
65² → 6 × 7 = 42 → 4225.
95² → 9 × 10 = 90 → 9025.
125² → 12 × 13 = 156 → 15625.

It works for every single one, and the algebra behind it is one line of expansion — which makes it a nice bridge into why identities are useful at all.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-3s): '65 squared. Two seconds. Go.'
RULE (3-12s): 'Digits before the five. Times the next number up. Then stick 25 on the end.'
DEMO (12-30s): '6 times 7 is 42. So 4225.' Then: 35² → 3×4=12 → 1225. 95² → 9×10=90 → 9025.
BIG ONE (30-40s): '125 squared? 12 times 13 is 156. 15,625.'
CTA (40-46s): 'Save it. Teach it. Watch a kid decide maths is a magic trick.'

subject: English
hook: The one-sentence rule that fixes 90% of school paragraphs.
body:
Every paragraph makes one point. If you can't say the point in one sentence, it's two paragraphs.

That's it. That's the whole rule, and it's the difference between an answer that reads like thinking and one that reads like a bucket.

Have your child underline the point sentence in each paragraph of their last essay. Where they can't find one, the marks went missing.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): 'One rule fixes ninety percent of school paragraphs.'
RULE (4-12s): 'Every paragraph makes ONE point. If you can't say the point in one sentence — it's two paragraphs.'
DEMO (12-28s): Show a bloated paragraph on screen. Split it. 'Same words. Now it reads like thinking instead of a bucket.'
HOMEWORK (28-40s): 'Take their last essay. Underline the point sentence in each paragraph. Where there isn't one — that's where the marks went.'
CTA (40-44s): 'Save this for the next assignment.'

subject: Science
hook: Weight is not mass, and this is the sentence that finally separates them.
body:
Mass is how much of you there is. Weight is how hard the planet is pulling on it.

On the Moon your child's mass is identical and their weight is one-sixth. Nothing about them changed. The planet did.

This is why the unit for mass is kg and the unit for weight is newtons — and why a numerical that mixes them up is the single most common lost mark in Grade 9 physics.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): 'Weight and mass are not the same thing, and one sentence separates them forever.'
SENTENCE (4-14s): 'Mass is how much of you there is. Weight is how hard the planet is pulling on it.'
DEMO (14-28s): 'On the Moon your mass is identical. Your weight is one-sixth. Nothing about YOU changed. The planet did.'
EXAM (28-40s): 'Which is why mass is kilograms and weight is newtons — and mixing them is the most common lost mark in Grade 9 physics.'
CTA (40-46s): 'Save it before the next physics test.'

subject: Mathematics
hook: The order maths actually breaks in, and where to look first.
body: A collapse in Grade 10 almost never starts in Grade 10. Work backwards through this chain and you'll usually find it in one evening.
slides: Maths breaks in a predictable order.
Work backwards down this chain. You'll find it in an evening.
GRADE 10 stuck on trigonometry?
→ Check ratio and proportion (Grade 7).
GRADE 9 stuck on algebra?
→ Check fractions and negative numbers (Grade 6).
GRADE 8 stuck on percentages?
→ Check decimals and place value (Grade 5).
The failing chapter is almost never the broken one.
Comment MATHS for the full diagnostic chain.

subject: General
hook: Six things that look like laziness and are not.
body: Almost every child called lazy is avoiding something specific. Naming it correctly changes what you do next.
slides: Six things that look like laziness.
None of them are.
'Won't start' — often doesn't know what the first step IS. Avoidance of ambiguity, not effort.
'Rushes everything' — finishing fast ends the discomfort faster.
'Says it's boring' — the most socially safe way a 13-year-old can say 'I can't do this'.
'Forgets the homework' — sometimes genuinely organisational. Sometimes convenient.
'Only does the easy questions' — protecting a self-image. Very common in bright children.
'Fine at home, silent in class' — the room is the variable, not the child.
Each one has a different fix. 'Try harder' fixes none of them.

subject: Science
hook: Your child revised for eight hours and dropped four marks. Here's where they went.
body: Lost marks sort into four types and each needs an opposite response. Sorting them takes twenty minutes and is worth more than the next eight hours.
slides: Eight hours of revision. Four marks lower.
Lost marks come in four types. Each needs an opposite fix.
DIDN'T KNOW IT → more revision. This is the only one extra hours fix.
KNEW IT, RAN OUT OF TIME → pacing. Fix with timed papers, not content.
KNEW IT, MISREAD THE QUESTION → command words. A vocabulary problem.
KNEW IT, ARITHMETIC SLIPPED → automaticity. Ten minutes a day, not more revision.
Three of the four get WORSE with more revision hours.
That's why the effort felt wasted. It was aimed at the wrong bucket.

subject: General
hook: What we do in week two, when the marks haven't moved yet.
body: Week two is where most tutoring arrangements quietly fail, because nothing visible has changed and everyone starts to doubt it.
slides: Week two is where most tutoring quietly fails.
Nothing visible has changed. Everyone starts to doubt it.
WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING: we're working below their grade, on the gap.
That work does not show up in this week's test. It shows up in week six.
WHAT WE SEND YOU instead of marks:
— what your child could not do on day one
— what they can do now
— what we're doing next, and why
Progress you can read before the marks arrive.
If we can't show you that in week two, be suspicious. Of anyone.

subject: Mathematics
hook: The 'book shut' rule, and why every session ends with it.
body: A child who can do a question with the example visible has not learned it. They have copied it. The difference only shows up in an exam hall.
slides: Every session ends the same way. Book shut.
Three problems. No example visible. No notes.
WHY: a child who solves with the example open has copied, not learned.
Recognition and retrieval live in different places. Only one is examined.
It is uncomfortable, and the discomfort IS the learning.
If they can't do it book-shut, we haven't finished — so we don't move on.
This is the single habit that most separates tutoring that works from tutoring that feels nice.
Ask any tutor: what does the last five minutes look like?

subject: English
hook: How an essay actually improves, in the order it happens.
body: English feels unfixable to parents because progress isn't visible line by line. It arrives in a fixed sequence, and knowing the sequence tells you where your child currently is.
slides: How an essay actually improves. In order.
English feels unfixable because progress isn't visible line by line.
STAGE 1 — Has a point. Most essays don't. This alone moves a grade.
STAGE 2 — Every paragraph serves that point. Nothing decorative survives.
STAGE 3 — Evidence, not assertion. Quote, then explain why it proves the point.
STAGE 4 — Handles a counter-argument without collapsing.
STAGE 5 — Sentence rhythm and vocabulary. This is LAST, not first.
Most students are pushed straight to stage 5. That's why 'use better words' never works.
Find which stage your child is on. Work on that one only.

subject: Mathematics
hook: Divide anything by 5 in your head: double it, move the point.
body:
Dividing by 5 is the same as multiplying by 2 and dividing by 10, and the second one is free.

340 ÷ 5 → 680 → 68.
85 ÷ 5 → 170 → 17.
1,240 ÷ 5 → 2,480 → 248.

Same for multiplying by 5: halve it, move the point the other way. 86 × 5 → 43 → 430.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): '340 divided by 5. Two seconds, no pen.'
RULE (4-13s): 'Double it. Move the decimal point. That's it.'
DEMO (13-28s): '340 doubled is 680. Move the point: 68.' Then 85 → 170 → 17. Then 1240 → 2480 → 248.
WHY (28-38s): 'It works because dividing by 5 IS multiplying by 2 and dividing by 10 — and dividing by 10 is free.'
FLIP (38-48s): 'Multiplying by 5? Halve it, move the point the other way. 86 times 5 — 43 — 430.'
CTA (48-52s): 'Save it. Test them at dinner.'

subject: Science
hook: The five words that fix almost every science definition.
body: Definitions lose marks not because the child doesn't know the idea, but because the sentence has no structure. These five words impose one.
slides: Five words that fix almost every science definition.
The idea is usually known. The sentence has no shape.
IS — start by naming the category. 'Osmosis IS the movement of...'
OF — say what it acts on. '...of water molecules...'
FROM / TO — give the direction. '...from high to low concentration...'
THROUGH — name the condition. '...through a partially permeable membrane.'
One sentence. Four marks. No memorised wording needed.
Try it on any definition in tonight's chapter.

subject: English
hook: Semicolons, settled in fifteen seconds.
body:
A semicolon joins two things that could each survive alone as a sentence.

'She revised for hours; the marks did not move.' Both halves stand up on their own. Semicolon is correct.
'She revised for hours; because she was worried.' The second half collapses. Semicolon is wrong — use a comma.

That's the entire rule. Everything else about semicolons is decoration.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): 'Semicolons. Fifteen seconds. Settled forever.'
RULE (4-13s): 'A semicolon joins two things that could each be a sentence on their own.'
RIGHT (13-26s): On screen: 'She revised for hours; the marks did not move.' 'Cover either half. Both stand up. Correct.'
WRONG (26-40s): 'She revised for hours; because she was worried.' 'Cover the first half. The second collapses. Wrong — use a comma.'
CLOSE (40-48s): 'That's the whole rule. Everything else is decoration.'

subject: Mathematics
hook: Six words in a maths question that tell you exactly what to do.
body: Exam boards use a fixed vocabulary. Children who know it stop guessing at what's being asked and start answering it.
slides: Six words that tell you exactly what the question wants.
Exam boards use a fixed vocabulary. Most students never learn it.
STATE / WRITE DOWN — no working needed. Just the answer. Don't waste time.
SHOW THAT — the answer is given. Marks are ONLY for the steps.
HENCE — you must use the previous part. Starting fresh scores zero.
DETERMINE / FIND — working required, method carries marks.
EXPLAIN — words, not numbers. A calculation alone gets nothing.
SKETCH vs PLOT — sketch is shape and key points. Plot means accurate scale.
Comment MATHS for the full command-word sheet.

subject: French
hook: Why 'je suis 14 ans' makes a French examiner wince.
body:
In French you don't 'be' an age, you 'have' one. J'ai quatorze ans — literally, I have fourteen years.

The same verb runs a whole family of expressions English gets wrong: j'ai faim (I have hunger), j'ai froid (I have cold), j'ai peur (I have fear), j'ai raison (I have reason — I'm right).

Learn the pattern once and six mistakes disappear together.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'Je suis quatorze ans. Every French examiner just winced.'
RULE (5-15s): 'In French you don't BE an age. You HAVE one. J'ai quatorze ans — I have fourteen years.'
FAMILY (15-35s): On screen: j'ai faim — I have hunger. j'ai froid — I have cold. j'ai peur — I have fear. j'ai raison — I have reason.
PAYOFF (35-45s): 'One pattern. Six mistakes gone at once.'
CTA (45-50s): 'Comment FRENCH for the vocabulary pack.'

subject: Coding
hook: Debugging, taught as a method instead of a mood.
body: Most children debug by staring harder and changing things at random. It's a procedure, and it can be taught in an afternoon.
slides: Debugging is a method, not a mood.
Most kids debug by staring harder and changing things at random.
1. READ the error. Out loud. It usually names the line and the problem.
2. PRINT the value just before it breaks. Assume nothing.
3. HALVE it. Comment out half the code. Which half still fails?
4. Repeat step 3 until the broken line is obvious.
5. Only THEN change something. One thing. Then re-run.
This is the same procedure a professional uses. It scales to any language.
Comment CODE for the parent primer.

subject: Public Speaking
hook: Nerves are not the enemy. Unrehearsed openings are.
body:
Almost all visible panic happens in the first fifteen seconds, before the speaker has found their footing.

So rehearse only the opening. Not the whole speech — the first three sentences, until they're automatic. Once those are out, the body of the talk usually looks after itself.

The rest of the nerves stay. They just stop showing.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'Nerves aren't the enemy. Unrehearsed openings are.'
OBSERVATION (5-18s): 'Almost all visible panic happens in the first fifteen seconds — before the speaker finds their footing.'
DRILL (18-33s): 'So rehearse ONLY the opening. Not the whole speech. The first three sentences, until they're automatic.'
PAYOFF (33-45s): 'Once those are out, the body of the talk looks after itself. The nerves stay. They stop showing.'
CTA (45-52s): 'Comment SPEAK for the drill sheet.'

subject: Mathematics
hook: Estimate first. It catches almost every calculator disaster.
body:
A mistyped digit turns 4.7 into 47 and nobody notices, because the calculator answers with total confidence.

So before pressing anything, round hard and say the rough answer out loud. 4.7 × 19.6 is 'about 5 times 20, so about 100'. If the screen says 921, you've found the typo before it cost you the mark.

Two seconds. It saves marks in every numerical paper a child will ever sit.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'Estimate first. It catches almost every calculator disaster.'
PROBLEM (5-16s): 'A mistyped digit turns 4.7 into 47 — and the calculator answers with total confidence.'
METHOD (16-32s): 'Before you press anything: round hard, say it out loud. 4.7 times 19.6 is about 5 times 20. About 100.'
CATCH (32-44s): 'If the screen says 921, you've found the typo before it cost you the mark.'
CLOSE (44-52s): 'Two seconds. Works in every numerical paper they'll ever sit.'

subject: Science
hook: Why ice floats, and why that one oddity is the reason you exist.
body:
Nearly every substance is denser as a solid. Water is not: the molecules lock into a lattice with gaps, so ice takes up more room than the water it froze from.

Which means lakes freeze from the top down, not the bottom up. A sheet of ice forms and insulates everything underneath it, so the water below stays liquid all winter.

If ice sank, ponds would freeze solid to the floor and take every living thing with them.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'Ice floats. That one oddity is the reason there's anything alive in a frozen lake.'
SCIENCE (5-20s): 'Almost every substance is denser as a solid. Water isn't — the molecules lock into a lattice WITH GAPS, so ice takes more room.'
CONSEQUENCE (20-36s): 'So lakes freeze from the TOP down. A sheet forms and insulates everything under it. The water below stays liquid all winter.'
STAKES (36-48s): 'If ice sank, ponds would freeze solid to the floor — and take every living thing with them.'
CTA (48-52s): 'Send this to a curious 12-year-old.'

subject: English
hook: Read the question twice. Genuinely twice. Here's what changes.
body:
On the first read a student is looking for what the question is about. On the second they see what it actually asks them to do — and those are different things far more often than anyone expects.

'Discuss how the writer presents grief' is not 'write about grief'. One is about technique, the other is about theme, and only one of them scores.

Twenty seconds. Usually worth more than the last hour of revision.

subject: General
hook: Changing boards mid-school: what actually transfers and what doesn't.
body: Families move countries and schools more than the syllabus designers assume. Here is where the seams show.
slides: Changing boards mid-school.
What transfers, and what quietly doesn't.
MATHS transfers well. Topics are ordered differently, but the content overlaps heavily.
SCIENCE transfers at content level; the PRACTICAL and coursework requirements often don't.
ENGLISH is the hardest jump. Set texts differ, and so does what an examiner rewards.
LANGUAGES: a CBSE French student meeting IGCSE speaking assessment is a real shock.
THE REAL GAP is assessment style, not knowledge.
Budget one term to learn the new exam, not the new subject.
Comment BOARDS for the comparison one-pager.

subject: General
hook: Predicted grades: how they're actually decided, and how to influence them honestly.
body: Predicted grades open or close university applications, and most families discover how they work about a year too late.
slides: Predicted grades decide which universities are even possible.
Most families learn how they work a year too late.
They are based on EVIDENCE the school already holds — mocks, classwork, internal assessment.
Not on potential. Not on how hard your child is trying now.
Which means the work that sets them happens 12-18 months before the prediction.
A weak mock in Year 12 can cap a Year 13 prediction.
HONEST influence: ask which pieces of evidence count, and when.
Then improve those specific pieces. That's it. There's no other lever.

subject: Mathematics
hook: Grade 10 to Grade 11 maths is a bigger jump than Grade 9 to 10. Here's the actual reason.
body: Every year the same shock: a child comfortable at 85% in Grade 10 struggles badly in Grade 11. It isn't difficulty. It's a change of species.
slides: Grade 10 → 11 maths is a bigger jump than 9 → 10.
A child at 85% in Grade 10 can genuinely struggle in Grade 11.
It isn't difficulty. The subject changes species.
GRADE 10 rewards PROCEDURE — recognise the type, apply the method.
GRADE 11 rewards STRUCTURE — choose the method, justify it, combine two.
Calculus arrives assuming algebra is automatic, not merely known.
Procedural students hit a wall the term calculus starts.
The prep isn't harder questions. It's unfamiliar ones, in Grade 10.

subject: General
hook: Mock exams are being used wrong in most houses.
body: A mock is not a prediction. It is the highest-quality diagnostic your child will get for free, and most of its value is thrown away within a week of the result.
slides: Mock exams are being used wrong in most houses.
A mock is not a prediction. It's a free, high-quality diagnostic.
THE MISTAKE: look at the mark, feel something, move on.
THE USE: go through the paper question by question and sort every lost mark.
BUCKET 1 — Didn't know it. That's revision.
BUCKET 2 — Knew it, ran out of time. That's pacing, and it's fixable fastest.
BUCKET 3 — Knew it, misread the question. That's command words.
BUCKET 4 — Knew it, arithmetic slipped. That's automaticity, not carelessness.
Four buckets need four different responses. The mark alone tells you none of it.
Comment EXAM for the sorting sheet.

subject: General
hook: Questions worth asking at a parent-teacher meeting, and three that waste it.
body: You get about eight minutes. Most of it usually goes on questions the report already answered.
slides: Parent-teacher meeting. You get about eight minutes.
Most of it goes on questions the report already answered.
DON'T ASK: 'How is she doing?' You have the grades. You're asking them to read them aloud.
DON'T ASK: 'Is he behaving?' It's a yes/no you'd already know if it were no.
DON'T ASK: 'What can we do at home?' Too broad. You'll get 'keep reading'.
DO ASK: 'Which specific topic is she weakest on right now?'
DO ASK: 'When he's stuck, what does he do — ask, guess, or stop?'
DO ASK: 'If you had one more hour a week with him, what would you use it on?'
That last one gets you the honest answer. It always does.

subject: Science
hook: Required practicals are free marks that most students donate back.
body:
In IGCSE and A-level sciences, a fixed set of practicals is examinable — and the questions are predictable: variables, control, error, improvement.

Students revise the theory and skip the practicals, then meet six marks on apparatus they last touched in October.

Go through each required practical and write four lines: what was measured, what was controlled, where the error came from, how you'd improve it. That's the whole exam question, every time.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'Required practicals are free marks. Most students donate them back.'
FACT (5-18s): 'In IGCSE and A-level science, a fixed set of practicals is examinable — and the questions are always the same four.'
THE FOUR (18-34s): On screen: What was MEASURED? What was CONTROLLED? Where's the ERROR? How would you IMPROVE it?
PROBLEM (34-44s): 'Students revise theory and skip practicals, then meet six marks on apparatus they last touched in October.'
CTA (44-52s): 'Four lines per practical. Do it this weekend.'

subject: Mathematics
hook: [STUDENT_FIRST_NAME] went from [START_MARK] to [END_MARK] in [SUBJECT]. Here is what actually changed.
body:
Not more hours. Fewer, better ones.

Week 1-2: we stopped teaching the current chapter entirely and went back to [GAP_CHAPTER].
Week 3-5: current chapter, but every session ended with three problems solved with the book shut.
Week 6-8: past papers, timed, marked by [MENTOR_NAME] in front of [STUDENT_FIRST_NAME] so the reasoning got corrected, not just the answer.

The marks moved in week six. The confidence moved in week two, and that was the part that mattered.
slides: [START_MARK] → [END_MARK] in [SUBJECT]. Eight weeks.
Not more hours. Fewer, better ones.
WEEKS 1-2: Stopped the current chapter. Went back to [GAP_CHAPTER].
WEEKS 3-5: Current chapter. Every session ends with 3 problems, book shut.
WEEKS 6-8: Timed past papers, marked live by [MENTOR_NAME].
Marks moved in week 6.
Confidence moved in week 2.
That was the part that mattered.

subject: General
hook: What one week of 1:1 actually looks like. No highlight reel.
body: Screenshots and notes from a real week with [STUDENT_FIRST_NAME], shared with [PARENT_NAME]'s permission.
slides: One real week of 1:1. Not a highlight reel.
MON — Diagnostic. We found the gap was [GAP_CHAPTER], not the chapter they were failing.
WED — 40 minutes on the gap. Zero minutes on the syllabus. Parent was nervous. We held.
THU — Parent note sent: what we found, what we're doing, what to expect.

What changed: nothing about effort. Everything about sequence.
This is what one mentor and one child can do that a batch of 40 cannot.
Shared with permission.

subject: Public Speaking
hook: Six weeks ago [STUDENT_FIRST_NAME] wouldn't read aloud in class. This is week six.
body:
The work was not 'confidence building'. It was reps, in this order:

subject: General
hook: The first session is not a class. It's a diagnosis.
body:
We don't start teaching in session one. We find out where the floor actually is.

That means working backwards through the chain — the chapter they're failing, the chapter under it, the skill under that — until we find the last thing they can do confidently.

That point is where teaching starts. Everyone else starts at the syllabus, which is why the same chapter gets re-taught three times and still doesn't land.

subject: General
hook: Why a batch of 40 cannot do what one mentor does. Structurally.
body: This isn't a criticism of school teachers. It's arithmetic.
slides: Why a batch of 40 can't do what one mentor does.
This isn't about teacher quality. It's arithmetic.
A 40-minute period ÷ 40 students = 60 seconds each. If nobody else speaks.
The teacher must move at the pace of the median child. By definition, half the room is in the wrong lesson.
A child who is lost cannot say so without cost. So they don't.
The syllabus must be finished. Gaps are carried forward, not closed.
1:1 changes exactly one variable: the pace is set by YOUR child.
Everything else — the diagnosis, the confidence, the marks — follows from that one change.

subject: English

The vocabulary barely changed. What changed is that the second answer has a point, and every sentence in it is doing a job for that point.

subject: General
hook: CBSE vs ICSE vs IGCSE, decided in one page instead of forty WhatsApp forwards.
body: There is no best board. There is a board that fits the child you actually have, and the country they are likely to study in.
slides: CBSE vs ICSE vs IGCSE. One page. No WhatsApp forwards.
There is no best board. There is a fit.
CBSE — Tighter syllabus, strong maths/science spine, aligned to JEE and NEET. Best if the child is India-bound and competitive-exam bound.
ICSE — Broader, heavier on English and internal assessment. Best for strong readers and writers, and children who like depth over speed.
IGCSE — Modular, application-led, internationally portable. Best if there's a chance of moving countries, or the child learns by doing.
The real question isn't which is hardest.
It's: which one matches how your child already learns?

subject: General
hook: MYP to DP is the hardest jump in the IB, and almost nobody prepares for it.
body: MYP rewards process, reflection and criteria. DP rewards content mastery under time pressure. A child fluent in one can be genuinely lost in the other for a whole term.
slides: MYP → DP is the hardest jump in the IB.
Almost nobody prepares for it. Here's why it hurts.
MYP marks you on criteria A-D. Process, inquiry, reflection.
DP marks you on content mastery, under time pressure, against a global cohort.
A child fluent in one can be lost in the other for an entire term.
THE THREE GAPS: 1) Volume of content per week roughly doubles.
2) Internal Assessment demands independent research design, not guided inquiry.
3) Maths AA vs AI is chosen at 16 and quietly decides which degrees stay open.
Start the bridge in MYP 5. Not in DP1 September.

subject: Mathematics
hook: Maths AA or AI? The choice your 16-year-old makes in ten minutes and lives with for four years.
body:
AA is analysis and proof. AI is application and modelling. Neither is easier — they're different subjects wearing the same name.

The filter that actually matters is the degree, because engineering and most economics courses want AA HL, and a wrong turn here closes doors quietly, two years before anyone notices.

AI — Applications & Interpretation. Modelling, statistics, real-world data.

Engineering, most Economics, many Physics courses → AA HL.

subject: General
hook: Internal assessment is not homework, and treating it like homework costs a grade.
body:
In IGCSE and IB, coursework and IAs carry a fixed share of the final grade and are marked against published criteria that the student is allowed to read.

Most students never read them. They write what they think is good, then get marked against what the criteria actually asked for.

One evening with the rubric, before the first draft, is worth more than three redrafts after.

subject: Science
hook: The CBSE Grade 10 Science paper rewards a specific kind of answer. Most students don't write it.
body: Marks are awarded per point, not per paragraph. A beautiful three-line explanation that contains one marking point scores one mark. Three ugly bullet points containing three marking points score three.
slides: The CBSE Grade 10 Science paper rewards one specific kind of answer.
Most students don't write it.
Marks are awarded PER POINT. Not per paragraph.
A beautiful 3-line explanation with 1 marking point = 1 mark.
Three ugly bullets with 3 marking points = 3 marks.
So: count the marks. Write that many distinct points.
5-mark question? Five points. Labelled diagram counts as one of them.
This isn't gaming the exam. It's reading the instructions.

subject: General

body:
Nothing about Grade 9 is examined externally, which is exactly why it gets treated as a buffer.

But Grade 10 assumes Grade 9 completely, and Grade 11 assumes Grade 10 completely. A gap opened here is compounding by the time anyone measures it.

The cheapest year to fix a child's maths is the year nobody is worried about it.

subject: English
hook: How an English examiner actually reads your child's answer.
body: Not word by word. In about ninety seconds, looking for specific evidence against a band descriptor.
slides: How an English examiner actually reads your child's answer.
Not word by word. In roughly 90 seconds.
They are hunting for evidence against a band descriptor.
FIRST — Is there a clear position in the opening lines? (Band decided, roughly, here.)
SECOND — Is each paragraph doing one job for that position?
THIRD — Is there textual evidence, or just assertion?
FOURTH — Does the vocabulary serve the point, or decorate it?
Which is why 'write more' is bad advice.
'Write with a position, and prove it' is the whole subject.

subject: General
hook: Three weeks to the board exam. Here is what actually moves marks now.
body:
At three weeks out, learning new chapters has a poor return. Three things don't:

Past papers under real time pressure, because most lost marks are pacing, not knowledge.
The error log — every mistake from the last month, re-attempted, no new questions.
One full sleep schedule, held, because a tired brain loses more marks than a weak chapter.
slides: Three weeks to the board exam.
Stop learning new chapters. The return is terrible now.
DO THIS INSTEAD —
1. Past papers. Real clock. Most lost marks are pacing, not knowledge.
2. The error log. Every mistake from the last month, re-attempted.
3. No new questions. None. Only the ones you got wrong.
4. A sleep schedule you actually hold.
A tired brain loses more marks than a weak chapter.

subject: French
hook: What DELF A2 actually asks a 14-year-old to do.
body: Parents hear 'French exam' and picture vocabulary lists. The exam is four skills, and the one that sinks students is the one nobody practises.
slides: What DELF A2 actually asks a 14-year-old to do.
Four papers. Equal weight. Most people prepare for one.
LISTENING — short everyday recordings, played twice, real speed.
READING — signs, emails, short articles. Skimming, not translating.
WRITING — two short texts. A message, and a simple account of an event.
SPEAKING — guided conversation, then a role-play with an examiner.
The one that sinks students: SPEAKING. Because nobody practises it out loud.
Vocabulary lists don't pass DELF. Twenty minutes of talking a week does.

That one substitution, made a hundred times over a term, is most of what you're paying for.
